Article Title: A 27-year-old from Melbourne who has been through more than 10 operations started a health charity at 21, and with 800 young volunteers and $500,000 raised he is now Victoria’s Young Australian of the
Article Text:
More than 800 young volunteers join the initiative

Personal health struggles shaped his mission

Four Victorians recognised in the 2027 awards

A personal experience with serious illness has inspired a young Australian to build a healthcare initiative that is now reaching communities across several countries. Ryan Brigham, 27, has been named Victoria’s 2027 Young Australian of the Year for founding Health in Focus, a charity that has brought together more than 800 young volunteers and raised over $500,000 for healthcare programmes. The announcement was made by the National Australia Day Council on November 12, with ABC News and the Victorian Government also reporting on his recognition. Brigham established Health in Focus (HIF) at the age of 21, driven by the belief that access to basic healthcare information and services should not depend on a person’s circumstances or where they live. The organisation works across Australia and internationally, delivering health initiatives and educational programmes aimed at addressing gaps in healthcare access. Its work has since expanded across Australasia, Southeast Asia and Africa, with thousands of patients, students and community members benefiting from its initiatives.One of the defining aspects of Health in Focus is its emphasis on involving young people in community healthcare. Rather than limiting its work to fundraising, the organisation gives volunteers opportunities to participate in planning and delivering programmes that respond to local health needs.With more than 800 volunteers involved, HIF has mobilised over $500,000 for its initiatives. The programmes cover different aspects of healthcare support and education, helping communities access resources that might otherwise be difficult to obtain.In Victoria, one of its key initiatives involves mobile cardiac screening clinics. These clinics provide free heart health assessments, with an emphasis on identifying potential cardiovascular problems early. The initiative is particularly important because cardiovascular disease remains a significant public health concern, and early detection can help people seek medical attention before complications become more serious.Brigham’s work is closely connected to his own experiences with illness. He has spent years dealing with serious health challenges, repeated hospital admissions and more than 10 operations. These experiences gave him firsthand insight into the difficulties people can face while navigating healthcare systems and reinforced his understanding of why access to medical support matters.His journey also shaped his decision to establish an organisation that could make healthcare information and basic support more accessible to people beyond traditional healthcare settings. At 27, Brigham’s recognition highlights how personal experiences can translate into wider community initiatives, particularly when young people are given opportunities to participate in meaningful social work.Brigham was among four recipients announced at the Victorian ceremony, with the awards recognising contributions across healthcare, research, advocacy and community service. Cherie Dear was named the 2027 Australian of the Year for Victoria for her work raising awareness and funding research into pancreatic cancer through the Dare to Hope initiative.Associate Professor Wenn Lawson received the Senior Australian of the Year award for his contributions to autism research, advocacy and education. Lawson, an autistic researcher and author, has spent decades advancing understanding of autism and neurodivergence. Gavin Hynam, known as Bear, was named Victoria’s Local Hero for his Cars 4 Youth programme. He helps young people in regional communities gain independence by repairing and gifting second-hand cars, while also mentoring learner drivers.The four Victorian recipients will join award winners from Australia’s other states and territories for the national Australian of the Year Awards, scheduled to be announced in Canberra on January 25, 2027.
Article Summary: Four Victorians recognised in the 2027 awards. Ryan Brigham, 27, has been named Victoria’s 2027 Young Australian of the Year. Brigham established Health in Focus at the age of 21, driven by the belief that access to basic healthcare information and services should not depend on a person's circumstances or where they live.

Article Title: An Indiana man agreed to give his former wife $35,000 from his retirement fund, then argued a later divorce agreement wiped out the promise; an appeals court upheld the transfer obligation and $2,500

Husband argued later agreement cancelled payment

Court upholds contempt finding and fees

An Indiana man who agreed to transfer $35,000 from his retirement savings to his former wife during divorce proceedings later argued that a subsequent settlement agreement had cancelled the obligation. However, the Indiana Court of Appeals upheld a contempt finding against him and the requirement to complete the transfer. In a November 25, 2026 memorandum decision , Russell Mangas v. Megan Mangas, available on Justia, the court also upheld an order requiring him to pay $2,500 towards his former wife's attorney fees.According to the court's decision, Russell Mangas filed for divorce from Megan Mangas in May 2023. The proceedings initially addressed the marital home, household bills, child custody, parenting time and child support. In February 2024, the couple entered into a property settlement agreement resolving their financial and property-related issues. This included the division of real estate, personal belongings, bank accounts and retirement savings.Under the agreement, Megan was entitled to receive $35,000 from Russell's Vanguard retirement account. He was also required to prepare a Qualified Domestic Relations Order (QDRO), a legal order used to divide retirement benefits between former spouses, to complete the transfer.The trial court approved the agreement. The couple subsequently entered into another agreement in June 2024 covering child custody and parenting arrangements.In December 2024, they signed a final bifurcated settlement agreement addressing the remaining matters, including child support, children's health insurance and extracurricular expenses.The December agreement included provisions stating that the parties had settled all contested issues, had no outstanding financial obligations and mutually released each other from further claims and liabilities. Russell later relied on these clauses to argue that his obligation to transfer the $35,000 had been extinguished.In January 2025, however, his former attorney had prepared and sent a draft QDRO to Megan, who signed and returned it. Russell never completed the document. In January 2026, Megan petitioned the trial court to find him in contempt for failing to execute the QDRO and transfer her share of the retirement account.The trial court held a hearing on April 2, 2026, despite Russell's request for a postponement. It found him in contempt, ordered his attorney to provide a new QDRO within seven days and directed him to pay $2,500 towards Megan's attorney fees. Russell appealed, arguing that the December agreement had eliminated his earlier financial obligation.The Indiana Court of Appeals examined whether the December agreement clearly cancelled the February property settlement. It acknowledged that some clauses in the later agreement appeared to support Russell's interpretation. However, the judges also considered its reference to the February agreement, which specifically stated that the earlier document had resolved the couple's financial issues.The court concluded that the December agreement could reasonably be interpreted in two ways. It was therefore ambiguous, allowing the trial court to consider evidence outside the document to establish the parties' intentions. The draft QDRO sent by Russell's former attorney in January 2025 was particularly relevant. The court found that this evidence supported the conclusion that the parties had not intended to cancel the $35,000 transfer obligation. It therefore upheld the contempt finding for his failure to complete the retirement transfer.Chief Judge Tavitas agreed with the outcome but issued a separate opinion. Unlike the majority, she considered the December agreement unambiguous, explaining that it preserved the earlier property settlement rather than cancelling it.Russell also challenged the trial court's decision to proceed with the hearing in his absence after denying his request for a postponement. He had requested a postponement one day before the scheduled hearing, explaining that he had misread the hearing date and was out of state for work. The appeals court found that he had not established sufficient grounds for another postponement and concluded that the trial court had not abused its discretion.On November 25, 2026, the Indiana Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's decision. The ruling leaves the requirement to complete the $35,000 retirement transfer and pay $2,500 towards Megan's attorney fees in place. The decision is a memorandum decision and, under Indiana Appellate Rule 65(D), is not binding precedent for other courts. It may be cited only for persuasive value or specified purposes, including res judicata, collateral estoppel and law of the case.

Article Title: A Florida woman transferred $1.85 million of her mother's money to people directed by an online scammer posing as a French billionaire; her brother sued, and a court upheld a $5.54 million judgment ag
Article Text:
Florida woman ordered to pay $5.54 million after transferring mother's money in online scamAI generated image using Canva

The brother’s lawsuit

What the record showed

A Florida appeals court has upheld a $5.54 million judgment against a woman who used a power of attorney to move nearly $1.85 million from her mother’s bank account to people directed by an online scammer posing as French billionaire Francois-Henri Pinault, as per details on Justia U.S Law. The Third District Court of Appeal affirmed the Miami-Dade trial court’s summary judgment on November 25, 2026, in a case brought by Kimberly Langston’s brother, Michael Burrows, over the loss of their late mother Sherry Burrows’ money.The decision does not erase the emotional complexity of romance fraud, but it makes clear that being deceived by a scammer does not automatically excuse a financial agent who transfers an elderly parent’s funds without verification, documentation, or a clear benefit to the parent. The court found that Langston, acting under a durable power of attorney, first sent the money to her personal account and then transferred it to unknown recipients at the impersonator’s direction. Read more details about this case, as per the court details on Justia U.S Law, here:According to the appellate opinion, Sherry Burrows signed a durable power of attorney in June 2013, naming her husband as agent and Kimberly Langston as successor agent.At some point, Langston became the agent with authority to manage her mother’s financial affairs. In March 2020, Langston emailed her brother to say that she had been defrauded by a man she met online who claimed to be Pinault, and that $1,845,740 of their mother’s money was gone.Langston testified that she became romantically involved with the impersonator after meeting him online. She did not dispute that she never met him in person or took steps to verify his identity while she was transferring her mother’s money to him and to other unknown individuals. The scammer convinced her that the money would be invested, according to the court’s account of the record.Before sending the funds to the unknown people, Langston transferred the money into her own personal bank account. When asked why, she had no explanation or reason for that intermediate transfer. The court treated that step as especially important because a power of attorney does not give an agent authority to transfer the principal’s property to the agent personally.Burrows sued Langston for exploitation of an elderly person, civil theft, breach of a promissory note, and unjust enrichment. He later moved for summary judgment on the exploitation and civil theft claims, relying on Langston’s admissions, deposition testimony, document responses, Wells Fargo bank records, a 2017 loan agreement, and an email he had sent to her.Langston argued that Burrows had not shown admissible evidence that their mother met Florida’s legal definition of an “elderly person,” and that he had not proved she acted with the required intent. Her opposition included only her written responses to interrogatories. The trial court rejected those arguments, granted summary judgment for Burrows, and entered a final judgment of $5,537,250 against her.Under Florida law, a person who proves by clear and convincing evidence that they were injured by theft or exploitation of an elderly person can recover three times their actual damages, along with attorney fees and costs. The statute also sets a minimum damages amount of $200.Why the court agreedThe appeals court first examined whether Sherry Burrows qualified as an elderly person under Florida’s exploitation statute. It found no dispute that she was over 60. The record also showed that she had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and had serious memory problems, including forgetting to take medication. Langston’s own messages described her mother’s illness and said that some days were good while others were bad.The court concluded that those facts supported a finding that Sherry’s ability to provide adequately for her own care and protection was impaired. It distinguished the case from a criminal precedent involving a victim who lived independently and had occasional forgetfulness. Here, the mother lived with Langston even though she wanted to return to Colorado, and her memory problems were serious enough to affect medication management.The court then turned to exploitation. Under the relevant Florida provision, exploitation can occur when an agent under a power of attorney breaches a fiduciary duty and causes an unauthorized transfer of property, particularly where the elderly person does not receive reasonably equivalent value in return. The court said a breach can arise from negligent conduct, although certain violations, such as fraud or intentional mismanagement, require more than negligence.The appellate court identified several undisputed facts supporting the trial court’s conclusion. Langston transferred the money to herself, then sent it to unknown people or entities. She failed to confirm the identity of the person she was communicating with, performed no due diligence on the supposed investments, and obtained no receipts, evidence, or proof that any investments existed.The court also noted that she continued making transfers without any return on earlier investments, despite having knowledge or suspicion that the activity was illegal. One alleged payment involved $420,000 for the supposed release of Pinault’s agent, who was said to have been stopped by U.S. Customs. The court described these circumstances as multiple grounds supporting a finding that Langston exploited her mother.Langston argued that she had verified the impersonator’s identity through one video call. But the court pointed to her own messages, in which she said she initially thought the person on Skype was Pinault but later believed the call used a silent clip from an older video. Even after developing those doubts, she continued sending large sums at the impersonator’s request.A warning for familiesThe case is a stark example of how romance scams can move from private heartbreak into family financial devastation. The scammer used a convincing public identity, an online relationship, and promises of investment to direct money out of an elderly woman’s account. The court’s ruling, however, focused on Langston’s conduct as a fiduciary, not on whether she personally intended to steal from her mother.For families managing an older relative’s finances, the practical lessons are straightforward. Verify any person requesting money through independent sources, never rely solely on video calls or online profiles, keep investment documentation, and avoid moving funds through a personal account. A power of attorney is a serious legal responsibility, and the person holding it must act in the principal’s best interest rather than following instructions from an unverified online contact.The appellate court affirmed the trial court’s judgment, leaving the $5,537,250 award in place subject to any timely motion for rehearing. The opinion underscores that Florida’s civil exploitation and theft laws can impose substantial financial consequences when a trusted agent sends an elderly person’s savings to strangers based on an online scam.
Article Summary: Florida woman ordered to pay $5.54 million after transferring mother's money in online scam. Kimberly Langston used a power of attorney to move nearly $1.85 million from her mother’s bank account to people directed by an online scammer posing as French billionaire Francois-Henri Pinault.

Article Title: A longtime cruise passenger sued Royal Caribbean over a $405 car cleaning bill after claiming Celebrity staff directed him to an open parking lot; the cruise line subsequently banned him and his wife
Article Text:
Port Canaveral cruise parking takes an unexpected turn for Celebrity Cruises passenger

Celebrity Cruises passenger seeks $405 reimbursement for car cleaning

Royal Caribbean passenger files arbitration demand over $405 car cleaning bill

Royal Caribbean gives longtime passenger a lifetime ban after lawsuit

Why the passenger believed the cruise line was responsible

The port authority's warning that vehicles were parked at owners' risk

Consumer advocate questions passenger's legal arguments

Florida court dispute could add legal fees to Royal Caribbean car wash case

Disclaimer: This article is based on a report by Michelle Couch-Friedman, founder of Consumer Rescue. The Times of India has not independently verified the passenger's account, the allegations concerning the vehicle or the status and outcome of the legal proceedings.

A parking arrangement that seemed like a minor inconvenience before a Caribbean holiday turned into an expensive dispute for a Florida couple. After returning from a seven-night cruise aboard Celebrity Apex, the passenger found his Ford Expedition covered in hardened white deposits that he believed were sea salt. He subsequently spent $405 on washing and detailing the vehicle before seeking reimbursement from Celebrity Cruises. When the company refused, he pursued the matter through arbitration before taking it to a small claims court. The dispute eventually had consequences far beyond the original bill. Royal Caribbean, Celebrity's parent company, informed the passenger and his wife that they were no longer welcome aboard its ships.Eric J. and his wife arrived at Port Canaveral in Florida to board Celebrity Apex for a seven-night Caribbean sailing. The couple had used the port's parking facilities for years, generally preferring the covered garage. On this occasion, however, the garage was full.Eric said he was directed towards an uncovered overflow parking area by people he believed were Celebrity Cruises employees. He parked his Ford Expedition there before taking a shuttle to the cruise terminal with his wife.Although he was unhappy about having to leave the vehicle outdoors, the couple proceeded with their holiday.The concern resurfaced when they returned. According to Eric, his vehicle was covered in hard white spots, which he identified as deposits of sea salt, according to Consumer Rescue. He believed prolonged exposure to the coastal conditions had affected the paintwork and wanted the marks removed before they caused further deterioration.According to Consumer Rescue, Eric initially spent $35 at a local car wash. The service did not remove the salt deposits to his satisfaction, prompting him to arrange professional detailing at home for another $370.Reportedly, Eric subsequently hired a mobile car detailing company to work on the vehicle. The service included professional handwashing and bug removal, along with other detailing work. The invoice came to another $370, bringing his total spending to $405.Once the work was completed, Eric was satisfied with the result. He then turned to Celebrity Cruises, asking the company to reimburse him for the two cleaning services. His argument was that the vehicle had been exposed to the conditions because he had followed directions given at the cruise terminal. The company suggested that he examine his cruise contract, which made clear that parking at the port was not included in the cruise arrangements.The parking facilities at Port Canaveral are operated by the Canaveral Port Authority, rather than Celebrity Cruises or its parent company, Royal Caribbean Group. The cruise line's position was that the responsibility for the parking arrangement did not fall within its contractual obligations.The refusal did not end Eric's attempt to recover the money. After examining his cruise agreement, he found a clause referring to arbitration and decided to approach the American Arbitration Association (AAA), an organisation that administers arbitration and mediation proceedings. He submitted a ‘Demand for Arbitration’ against Royal Caribbean, including photographs of the vehicle, his parking receipt, the two cleaning bills and a copy of his cruise contract. He also paid a $225 filing fee to initiate the process.According to Consumer Rescue, the AAA required Royal Caribbean to pay a further $375 fee before the complaint could proceed. By this stage, the dispute had grown beyond the original cleaning expense, with the combined fees and detailing costs taking the amount involved above $1,000.However, the AAA did not proceed with the complaint. About a month after Eric submitted his demand, its Consumer Filing Team informed him that it would not administer the case. Its communication said either party could choose to take the dispute to the appropriate court.Soon after filing the paperwork, he received a telephone call from someone identifying himself as a Royal Caribbean representative. Eric initially thought the company might finally be contacting him to discuss compensation or settle the disagreement. Instead, he was informed that he and his wife had been permanently banned from sailing with Royal Caribbean and its affiliated cruise brands.For Eric, the announcement was particularly difficult to accept because of his history with the company. He told Consumer Rescue that he had been sailing with Royal Caribbean for more than 20 years and had never previously encountered a problem. He and his wife were members of the Crown and Anchor Society's Diamond-level loyalty programme and frequently travelled in suites.The ban meant losing the privileges accumulated through those years of cruising. Eric described the situation as a misunderstanding and hoped the company would reconsider its decision.Eric later approached consumer advocate Michelle Couch-Friedman, founder of Consumer Rescue, asking for assistance in getting the ban reversed. In his account, he maintained that Celebrity's customer service team had directed him to the contract when he sought compensation. He believed the contract's dispute-resolution provisions meant that arbitration was the appropriate next step. When the AAA declined to administer the case, he understood its response to mean that court proceedings were the remaining option.He also argued that the cruise line had failed to respond to the arbitration notice, leaving him with little choice but to continue with the claim. In correspondence shared with Couch-Friedman, he said the couple had followed the procedures set out in their agreement and had not expected to be banned for doing so.Eric indicated that he was prepared to withdraw the claim if that would help restore his relationship with the cruise line. He wanted his previous customer status and associated benefits back.Couch-Friedman contacted the Canaveral Port Authority to establish who operated the parking facilities and what responsibility it accepted for vehicles left there. The authority confirmed that passengers using its parking areas received a disclaimer printed on the reverse of their payment receipts. It stated that the authority was not responsible for vehicles or personal belongings, including losses or damage resulting from circumstances such as adverse weather.Eric had submitted a copy of his parking receipt as part of his evidence. The front identified the Canaveral Port Authority as the parking operator. According to Couch-Friedman's account, the document therefore raised a fundamental problem with his decision to pursue Royal Caribbean over the incident. The parking was not operated by Celebrity, and the receipt contained a warning that vehicles were left at the owner's risk. The claim also relied on Eric's belief that cruise employees had directed him to the outdoor facility, something that did not establish that the cruise line operated or controlled the parking area.The $370 detailing invoice described a deluxe cleaning service, including bug removal and work intended to improve the vehicle's appearance and protect it against the elements.Couch-Friedman said she could not establish why Royal Caribbean should be responsible for the cost of cleaning a vehicle parked in a facility operated by the port authority. She also challenged Eric's interpretation of the AAA communication. The association had said it would not administer the case and that either party could take the dispute to court. It had not instructed him to file a lawsuit, nor had Royal Caribbean advised him to pursue legal action over the cleaning bill.During their exchanges, Couch-Friedman raised the possibility that artificial intelligence might have influenced the way Eric was handling the complaint. She said she had encountered other consumer disputes involving legal-sounding arguments and demands that appeared to rely on incorrect information generated by AI tools.Eric did not confirm or deny using AI when she asked him directly. He continued to maintain that he had followed the instructions provided by the cruise line and the arbitration organisation. Couch-Friedman eventually told him that she considered the complaint to be without a sound basis and could not help him secure a reversal of the ban while the lawsuit remained active.Despite the consumer advocate's assessment, Eric did not agree to abandon his position. In a later message, he again said he was willing to withdraw the claim in the hope of repairing the relationship with Royal Caribbean. The case was still on the court docket at the time of Couch-Friedman's report. She said she would be interested to see whether Royal Caribbean sent its lawyers to contest the matter. She also pointed out that Florida courts can, in certain circumstances, order a plaintiff to pay the defendant's legal fees if a lawsuit is found to be frivolous.For the couple, the disagreement had moved a long way from the original $405 expenditure. What began as a complaint about an uncovered parking space had developed into a small claims dispute and a permanent exclusion from Royal Caribbean, Celebrity Cruises and Silversea. Whether the cruise line will reconsider the ban remains uncertain.

Article Title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan seeks execution delay, says he was defending Taliban
Article Text:
File photo: Nidal Hasan, charged with killing 13 people and wounding 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree at Fort Hood

Hasan wants to revive defence barred at trial

What happened in the Fort Hood attack?

Execution controversy and survivors’ objections

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution, saying he intends to argue that he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.In a court filing signed by Hasan on Tuesday, he said he intended to demonstrate that the military court’s judgment and his death sentence had been obtained and were being maintained in violation of his federal constitutional and statutory rights.The filing could delay the Trump administration’s plans to execute Hasan on December 3. A hearing has been scheduled for Wednesday morning.Hasan, who is representing himself with assistance from lawyers at the American Civil Liberties Union’s Capital Punishment Project, said he intended to continue representing himself in the legal fight.One of Hasan’s central arguments is that he was prevented from presenting a defence that his actions were legally justified because he was trying to protect the Afghan Taliban from what he described as an unlawful attack by the US Army.Hasan had argued that he was acting in “defense of others”, according to court documents. However, the military judge barred him from presenting that argument during his 2013 trial.After dismissing his lawyers and choosing to represent himself, Hasan largely remained silent during the three-week trial.While the military called nearly 90 witnesses, Hasan called none in his defence and made no closing argument.A military jury found him guilty of multiple counts of murder and attempted murder for the shooting, which left 13 people dead and 32 wounded.The case has been assigned to US district judge Tony Mattivi in Kansas, where Hasan is being held at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth. Mattivi was nominated by president Donald Trump and confirmed by the Senate in June.On November 5, 2009, Hasan walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at Fort Hood, Texas, where soldiers were waiting for medical tests and preparing for deployment.He opened fire with a handgun fitted with laser sights, killing 13 people and wounding more than 30 others.Hasan was shot by law enforcement officers during the attack, leaving him paralysed from the waist down and confined to a wheelchair.He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death.Trump authorised Hasan’s execution on the recommendation of defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, would be the first US military execution by firing squad since World War II and the first military execution since 1961.The plan drew controversy after Hegseth announced that the execution would be public and the Pentagon confirmed it would be livestreamed. Critics from both parties raised concerns that broadcasting the execution could fuel radicalisation and turn it into a spectacle.Trump later said the execution would not be livestreamed, but that immediate family members of the victims could witness it in person if they chose.The latest court filing comes amid further dispute over who will be allowed to attend. Military officials have denied requests from three survivors of the 2009 shooting to witness the execution, citing regulations, security and space constraints.The survivors argued that the military should recognise them as victims under a broader definition that includes direct physical, emotional or financial harm. The Army rejected their appeal, saying regulations specify who may attend a military execution.
Article Summary: Nidal Hasan killed 13 people and wounded 31 in a November 2009 shooting spree. He was convicted by a military jury in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder. The jury sentenced him to death and he was due to be executed on December 3. Hasan has asked a federal court to delay his scheduled execution. He intends to argue he was defending the Taliban from an unlawful US military attack.

Article Title: From Pokhran to partnership: Strobe Talbott’s Indian legacy
Article Text:
FILE - Strobe Talbott, President Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin. (AP Photo)

TOI Correspondent from Washington

Poll Vote & Share your view Should diplomats prioritize long-term relationships over immediate agreements? Yes, relationships are more important No, agreements count the most 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

: Strobe Talbott, who died on Thursday at 80, belonged to a vanishing breed of American diplomats for whom foreign policy was as much an exercise in understanding other countries as in advancing their own, a principle that is anathema in the crass MAGA era. Brilliant, cerebral, and possessed of an almost old-fashioned faith in dialogue, he helped accomplish something that, in the summer of 1998, seemed improbable: turning one of the worst crises in US-India relations into an opening for one of Washington’s most consequential strategic partnerships. Indeed, his most enduring diplomatic achievement was not a “deal” he signed or a war he “solved.” It was something more elemental: helping two countries that had spent decades talking past each other to begin talking to each other – respectfully.The story began in the unforgiving aftermath of the Shakti nuclear tests in May 1998, when the Clinton administration reacted with fury to what it saw as India’s imprudence. Sanctions followed, relations deteriorated, and the U.S pressed New Delhi to abandon its nuclear ambitions, sign the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) and accept the existing international non-proliferation architecture that would cap and roll back its nuclear program.India, under PM Vajpayee, was equally determined not to surrender what it regarded as an indispensable security imperative.Into this diplomatic minefield stepped Talbott, then Deputy Secretary of State -- also previously a Bill Clinton homie at Oxford and a former Time correspondent in Moscow -- and Jaswant Singh, India's principal interlocutor and subsequently External Affairs Minister. What followed was an extraordinary diplomatic marathon, stretching from 1998 to 2000, involving 14 meetings in seven countries, difficult arguments, private exchanges, family dinners in each others’ homes, and, eventually, a degree of mutual trust that neither side could have anticipated. It was a relationship that transcended the negotiating table.The talks did not produce the treaty (CTBT) Washington initially wanted, nor did it accept the American premise that India’s nuclear status was negotiable. But Talbott understood that diplomacy need not always end in agreement to be consequential. In an interview with this correspondent in January 1999, ahead of his eighth round of talks in New Delhi, he described his exchanges with Singh as an exercise in the “art of the possible. ” He also revealed that Clinton himself was the primary driver in the effort to repair ties, having read British Indian history as a Rhodes scholar at Oxford, and he was among the first to recognize India’s tech promise because of the y2k issue.Among the books scattered on the table in his office was Jaswant Singh’s “Defending India,” revealing that he was not merely negotiating with New Delhi; he was trying to understand it. Indeed, in Singh, he met an equally formidable diplomat, and the two men developed a friendship rooted in mutual respect, shared intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of each other's national compulsions. Their discussions were not confined to nuclear warheads, missile trajectories and non-proliferation benchmarks. They ranged across history, philosophy, international affairs and the larger question of how two democracies, with very different strategic experiences, could learn to trust each other.The significance of their engagement became apparent during the 1999 Kargil conflict, when Washington took a firm position against Pakistan's military adventurism, their talks aiding better American understanding of India's security concerns. Clinton's landmark visit to India in March 2000 was another milestone. The two countries were no longer simply managing a nuclear disagreement; they were on track for a substantially different relationship.The transformation would take several more years, with the Bush administration's decision to pursue nuclear cooperation with India, culminating in the landmark 2005 nuclear deal, being the crowning moment of this process. But it was the diplomatic groundwork laid by Talbott and Singh that helped establish the proposition that India's nuclear status could be accommodated within a broader strategic partnership rather than remain an eternal obstacle to it.For Talbott, the India engagement was also personal. His affection and admiration for Singh were evident long after both men had left office. When Jaswant Singh died in August 2020, Talbott's tribute was among the most touching. “Extraordinary man, wise and principled servant for his country and the world, brave soldier, honorable statesman, diplomat of finesse and effectiveness, author of wide scope, proud, loved, and loving husband and father, and friend. RIP.” he wrote. Well might every word apply to him.
Article Summary: Strobe Talbott helped turn one of the worst crises in US-India relations into an opening for one of Washington’s most consequential strategic partnerships. Talbott belonged to a vanishing breed of American diplomats for whom foreign policy was as much an exercise in understanding other countries as in advancing their own.

California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons, accusing President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals.He alleged that clemency had become a business under the Trump administration.In a post on X, Newsom said, "No president should be able to sell a pardon. Today, I’m calling for sweeping federal reform of the presidential pardon power. The Justice Department is not Donald Trump’s personal law firm. Justice is NOT for sale."In a video message accompanying the post, Newsom criticised MAGA supremo for delivering remarks at the department of justice (DOJ) alongside Attorney General Pam Bondi, who previously served as his personal defence lawyer."Today, Donald Trump is once again standing inside the Department of Justice next to his former personal defence lawyer, who is now the Attorney General, giving a speech about protecting American families," Newsom said.Questioning Trump's record on criminal justice, Newsom referred to the 1989 case involving five Black and Latino teenagers who were wrongfully accused of raping and assaulting a woman in New York's Central Park.The teenagers, later known as the Central Park Five, were exonerated after DNA evidence and a confession by another individual established their innocence."In 1989, you took out full-page ads screaming for the death penalty for five Black and Latino teenagers before a trial, before a shred of evidence. They were innocent. DNA proved it. You never apologised," Newsom said.The California governor also defended his own clemency decisions, insisting that individuals on the state's former death row would remain behind bars for life."To the families standing with him today, your grief is real. That's why every person, every person on California's former death row will die in prison. No one walks out," he said, contrasting his approach with Trump's use of presidential pardons.Newsom alleged that several individuals convicted of serious offences had received presidential pardons after making financial contributions or benefiting from personal connections involving Trump's political circle.Citing specific cases, he alleged that a billionaire facing bribery charges had secured a pardon after his family arranged a $50 million deal involving Trump's lawyer. He also claimed that an individual convicted of stealing $10 million from nursing home workers received clemency after his mother attended a million-dollar dinner at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.Newsom also criticised Trump's decision to pardon former Blackwater security contractors convicted in connection with the 2007 killing of 14 Iraqi civilians, including two children, in Baghdad.He further referred to the pardon of a participant in the January 6 Capitol riot who subsequently pleaded guilty to soliciting what he believed was a 15-year-old girl for sex. Newsom also criticised Trump's pardon of a foreign leader accused of facilitating large-scale cocaine trafficking into the United States."Nearly two billion, nearly $2 billion owed to victims and their families, gone. His own pardon attorney said it out loud: 'No MAGA left behind'," Newsom alleged.Accusing Trump of applying different standards of justice based on an individual's wealth and political connections, Newsom said, "Donald Trump doesn't oppose mercy. He sells it. If you're poor, Black, or Brown, you get the needle. If you're rich and know Donald Trump, you get a pardon and a personal phone call."He also raised concerns over Trump's remarks suggesting that more pardons could be forthcoming, including his statement that the possibility of pardoning himself was not unreasonable."A Justice Department that prosecutes his enemies and pardons himself and his friends? That's not law enforcement. That's a protection racket," Newsom said.Calling for structural changes to presidential clemency powers, Newsom said reforms were needed to prevent future presidents from using their constitutional authority to grant pardons for personal or financial benefit."We need foundational federal reform, starting with this: no president can ever again turn the power of mercy into a business. No president and no one should be able to sell a pardon," he said.Concluding his video message, the California governor reiterated that the Justice Department must function independently and serve the American people."A Justice Department is not Donald Trump's law firm. Justice is not for sale--not in California, and not in America," Newsom added.Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates, including individuals convicted of murdering children.Speaking at the Department of Justice on Monday (local time), Trump described Newsom's decision as one of the most shocking acts of injustice in the country. He accused the Governor and what he termed the Radical Left of prioritising convicted criminals over victims and their families."We're here today to talk about one of the most shocking acts of injustice our country has ever seen... Just days ago, the Governor of California, Gavin Newsom, granted clemency and mercy to 548 of the most EVIL monsters on the face of the Earth," Trump said.The US President also announced a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for individuals convicted of murdering children, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims."I will sign a Presidential Directive ordering the DOJ to seek the death penalty for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims. My order also directs the Attorney General to expedite the execution of federal death sentences. Once juries have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain," Trump said.He also referred to an executive order signed on the first day of his administration, directing the DOJ to pursue capital punishment for individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers.Trump further announced nearly $150 million in public safety grants to support the recruitment of more than 1,000 additional sworn law enforcement officers and improve responses to domestic violence and sexual assault cases.Additionally, he backed a legislative proposal introduced by Representative Brandon Gill, titled the 'Just Punishment for Murder Act'.The proposal seeks to strengthen capital punishment provisions and expand their application to individuals convicted of murdering law enforcement officers and illegal immigrants accused of murder.
Article Summary: California governor Gavin Newsom has called for sweeping federal reforms to the US president's power to grant pardons. He accused President Donald Trump of using the Justice Department to protect wealthy allies and politically connected individuals. Newsom's remarks came after Trump sharply criticised the California Governor over his decision to grant clemency to 548 death row inmates.

Article Title: 'Only winter will come': Bangladesh minister doubts Hasina will return in December
Article Text:
Hasina won't return in December, will be brought back in handcuffs: Bangladesh minister

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs on Thursday expressed doubt over the possibility of former PM Sheikh Hasina returning to the country in December this year. He sarcastically said that "only winter, and not the ousted leader, would arrive," news agency IANS reported.Tarique Rahman's aide reiterated that Hasina could return only through the extradition process under the existing treaty with India."I have already said at a meeting in Sylhet that Sheikh Hasina will not come in December……nobody will come in December; only winter will come,” United News of Bangladesh (UNB) quoted Kobir as saying.Kobir made the remarks while speaking to reporters at the ministry of foreign affairs in Dhaka.He said Bangladesh had already approached the relevant authorities in India seeking Hasina's handover under the extradition treaty.Bangladesh minister maintained that Hasina would have to be brought back in handcuffs or under strict surveillance to face trial, pointing out this as the only route for her return. He added that the request also covered other individuals accused of committing crimes in Bangladesh, UNB reported.The remarks come amid reports that Hasina, who has been living in exile in India, wishes to return to Dhaka aboard a state aircraft on December 16, coinciding with Bangladesh's Victory Day, which marks the country's liberation from Pakistan.Kobir had made a similar statement on Tuesday while responding to questions from journalists after briefing foreign diplomats in Dhaka. Rejecting reports about Hasina's proposed return, he said she could come back only as a prisoner to face justice."This news may be shown and shown by paying money. But we have to distinguish between reality and desire. The reality is that terrorists will be brought back to the country only to face justice. Some may have a wish, some may have nightmares while lying in their bedroom, that they are coming to the airport, boarding a train. But they are not ordinary passengers. They can only be brought back to the country in handcuffs or to face justice. That is the point,” Bangladesh's leading Bengali daily Prothom Alo quoted Kobir as saying.Earlier this month, Hasina asserted that the possibility of arrest, imprisonment or even death would not stop her from returning to Bangladesh. She said she would rather die in her homeland than remain away from her people.In a rare audio interview with news agency IANS, Hasina said she was aware of the risks but had never allowed fear to dictate her decisions. Recalling her previous returns to Bangladesh amid political uncertainty, she said she had faced imprisonment and repeated attempts on her life.“Look, I understand the risks very well. I may be arrested the moment I arrive. They may send me to prison. They may even try to kill me. I have considered all these possibilities. But, you know, I stopped worrying about my personal safety a long time ago. I returned to Bangladesh in 1981, despite military rule. I returned again in 2007, knowing that the military-backed government might arrest me. I have faced imprisonment and repeated attempts on my life. Fear has never stopped me from doing what I believe is right,” she said.Hasina has also reportedly sought a government aircraft to fly her back to Bangladesh.
Article Summary: Sheikh Hasina won't return in December, will be brought back in handcuffs: Bangladesh minister. He sarcastically said that "only winter, and not the ousted leader, would arrive" Tarique Rahman's aide reiterated that Hasina could return only through the extradition process under the existing treaty with India.

Article Title: New Haven agrees to pay $30 million to George Gould, who spent nearly 27 years in prison, and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who died in 2011, after their convictions in a 1993 murder were thrown out
Article Text:
New Haven's $30 million settlement awaits committee review and Board of Alders approval for borrowing.

Two men convicted in a 1993 murder

A lengthy legal battle before exoneration

$30 million settlement and approval process

Wrongful-conviction settlements reach $77 million

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

More lawsuits remain unresolved

Nearly three decades behind bars, a conviction that unravelled years later and a settlement worth millions of dollars have brought two wrongful-conviction cases in Connecticut closer to a conclusion. The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. While Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement, reported by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.Gould and Taylor were convicted of felony murder and other charges in connection with the July 4, 1993, killing of Eugenia Vega inside her Grand Avenue bodega in New Haven.According to the New Haven Independent, the prosecution's case relied heavily on testimony from a woman who claimed to have witnessed the crime. She later revealed that she had been arrested for prostitution and interrogated while experiencing severe heroin withdrawal.She alleged that police offered to help her obtain heroin in exchange for providing the statement they wanted. Investigators reportedly found no physical evidence linking either Gould or Taylor to the killing.Years later, two relatives reportedly approached the FBI and said Vega's son had confessed to them that he had killed his father, bringing fresh scrutiny to the convictions.The men's legal struggle involved multiple court proceedings. In 2010, a Connecticut Superior Court judge granted their habeas corpus petitions on grounds of actual innocence and ordered their release.However, the state appealed, and the Connecticut Supreme Court subsequently overturned that decision. During a second habeas proceeding, their petitions were denied, the online report adds.Gould returned to prison in 2011, while Taylor was allowed to remain at home because of his terminal cancer diagnosis. He died in October 2011, after spending more than 16 years incarcerated, New Haven Independent reported.Gould continued challenging his conviction and was released in 2021 after a judge modified his sentence. The state's Conviction Integrity Unit later reviewed the case, and prosecutors moved to vacate both convictions in 2024.The agreement was reached on November 13 in two consolidated federal civil rights cases against the city, the report added.Under the settlement, Gould will receive $18 million, while Taylor's estate, administered by Mary Murphy-Taylor, will receive $12 million. The latter payment remains subject to approval by the New Haven Probate Court.According to the Hartford Courant, the agreement also requires approval from the city's Litigation Settlement Committee. The New Haven Board of Alders must subsequently approve borrowing for the settlement.The New Haven Independent reported that Gould's legal representatives include Neufeld Scheck Brustin Hoffmann & Freudenberger, the Law Offices of Richard Emanuel and the Law Office of Attorney Michael A. Jefferson.The latest agreement represents the fourth and fifth federal civil rights lawsuits New Haven has settled within three months. Earlier settlements involved Adam Carmon for $16.5 million, Vernon Horn for $15.25 million and Marquis Jackson for $15.25 million.Together, the five settlements total $77 million. According to city officials cited by the New Haven Independent and Hartford Courant, borrowing to finance the payments could result in at least $116 million in repayments over 20 years when interest is included.Mayor Justin Elicker has acknowledged the city's responsibility to address past injustices while raising concerns about the financial burden on taxpayers. He has also called for the state to share more of the costs, noting that state authorities appealed the original decision granting Gould and Taylor relief.The mayor's office has pointed to the city's lack of insurance coverage for this type of incident in 1993 and the financial implications of settling claims decades later.The financial consequences may not end with the latest agreement. According to the New Haven Independent, lawsuits involving former Alder Troy Streater and Charles Coleman Jr. remain outstanding, alongside the separate case involving Stefon Morant, in which a jury previously awarded $38 million against the city. New Haven is appealing that verdict.For Gould, the settlement brings an end to a legal struggle that continued long after his release. For Taylor's family, the compensation comes years after his death and the eventual overturning of his conviction.The agreement represents another step in addressing wrongful convictions from New Haven's past, while leaving the city to confront the continuing legal and financial consequences.Image Courtesy: George Gould (right), with the late Ronald Taylor (center). Credit: Thomas MacMillan photo
Article Summary: The city of New Haven has agreed to pay $30 million to George Gould and the estate of Ronald Taylor, who were imprisoned for a 1993 murder they did not commit. Gould will receive $18 million after spending almost 27 years incarcerated, while Taylor's estate is set to receive $12 million following his death in 2011. The settlement marks another major financial resolution for the city as it faces mounting lawsuits linked to wrongful convictions dating back several decades.

Article Title: A sister stuck in Riyadh, a family waiting in India: The human cost of Saudi flight ban
Article Text:
Packed and waiting: The families stuck behind the Saudi flight ban

A route that keeps closing

The conflict behind the cancellations

Yemen's Houthi rebels and their areas of control

A sister in Riyadh and a journey that grew longer

A thick plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia (Image: Reuters)

Fear, then a fragile calm in Kuwait

Families watching the news from India

Safety against salary

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Waiting on a date

Indian airlines have again extended their cancellations to Saudi Arabia as conflict in the region continues. For families on both sides of the route, the delay has meant missed visits, longer journeys and a constant worry about what comes next.For Indian families with relatives in Saudi Arabia, planning a trip home now begins with a question no booking page can answer: when will the planes fly again?Air India and Air India Express have extended the suspension of their flights to and from Jeddah until November 30, citing the security situation in Saudi Arabia. Jeddah services had earlier been cancelled until November 24, while flights to Riyadh and Dammam were already cancelled until November 30."Due to the prevailing situation in the region, Air India and Air India Express flights to and from Jeddah, Dammam and Riyadh will remain suspended until 30 November 2026," Air India said in a post on X on Monday.The other Indian carriers on the route have taken similar steps. On November 18, IndiGo extended the cancellation of flights connecting Saudi Arabian cities until November 30. Akasa Air has cancelled its flights to and from Riyadh and Jeddah until the same date.With four airlines grounding the same routes for the same period, families who depend on direct flights have few easy options left.The suspensions follow months of escalating violence. In recent months, various Saudi Arabian cities and infrastructure have come under attack from the Houthis, the Iran-aligned group fighting the Saudi-backed government in Yemen. Since the fighting with the kingdom escalated over the summer, the Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi oil facilities, including the Jazan refinery, which was attacked again in the latest incident. Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said an attack on an oil refinery in the kingdom's southwest killed a Nepalese worker.The latest incidents mark a further escalation, with strikes from both sides targeting airports, energy facilities and other civilian and economic infrastructure.The violence is not one-sided. Saudi airstrikes hit western and southwestern Yemen overnight, according to Houthi officials and media. Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesperson for the Houthi-run health ministry, said multiple strikes across Taiz province killed four people, including a child, and blamed Saudi Arabia. The Associated Press said it could not independently verify the claims made by al-Asbahi or by Al-Masirah, the rebel-run television channel.Residents of Sanaa, the rebel-held capital, described a life of recurring explosions. "We have to endure these sounds every now and then, and they have health implications for our kids," said Khalil al-Makhlafi, who lives in the southern part of the city, near military camps.The conflict could widen further. The Houthis threatened to attack Saudi ports if the Yemeni port of Hodeidah came under attack. "The port of Hodeidah handles 90 percent of imported goods into Yemen. If it is closed, it could bring the humanitarian situation to the brink of collapse," said Al Jazeera's Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa.For Saad, the effect of the flight ban is personal. His sister and her husband live in Riyadh. They were supposed to travel to India because of a family emergency, but could not.Their only option was to go to Dubai from Riyadh and take a flight from there. "Usually it's a 5-6 hour journey which would have taken more than 20 hours. So they postponed it," Saad said.The couple is still in Riyadh, and the delay has left the family caught between two worries. "They're still stuck there since they can't make it to India. There's also a worry that if they do come, they won't be able to return because of the tense situation," he said.Saad said his sense of the risk has changed as the conflict has moved closer to the city. "The situation previously remained manageable as strikes were confined to refineries and airports located at a distance from the urban center. However, the landscape has shifted with recent targeting of central city locations, leading to heightened apprehension," he said.He now speaks to his sister more often than he used to. "I make it a point to call her twice daily to ensure that she is doing well," he said.The effects of the conflict are felt beyond Saudi Arabia. A man from India who works in Kuwait told TOI that the regional conflict upended his plans too.He last travelled from Kuwait to India on September 26, 2025, and returned in November 2025. His next trip was planned for March 2026, a short vacation during Holi. "Unfortunately, the conflict started around the same time, and I had to cancel my travel plans," he said.He said Kuwait International Airport was affected by a drone attack around that period, which disrupted operations. Terminal 4 later partially resumed, but flights were limited to certain destinations, and ticket prices were extremely high. "Naturally, there was considerable panic among the public, especially among expatriates who wanted to return to their home countries," he said.Kuwait's distance from Iran, approximately 180 to 200 kilometres, added to the anxiety. People worried about possible escalation, and safety advisories and precautionary guidelines were being circulated.Mobile phone alerts became part of daily life. "Whenever there was an air threat, emergency sirens would sound on our phones. Sometimes, we received these alerts several times during the night, even around 20 times," he said.He credits the authorities with keeping the country running. Air defence systems intercepted incoming threats, and the government maintained food supplies, accommodation arrangements and other essential services. There were some concerns about water supply and possible communication disruptions after damage to undersea fibre-optic cables, but he said these did not significantly affect daily life."Initially, there was certainly fear and uncertainty. However, I believe the Kuwaiti authorities handled the situation responsibly," he said. "At present, I feel much more comfortable compared to the initial period of the conflict. From what I can see, the threat level has reduced significantly, and our daily life and work are almost back to normal."He added that people still follow official safety instructions. "Of course, we remain alert and follow official safety instructions, but I do not feel the same level of panic that we experienced initially," he said.For relatives at home, news bulletins have been harder to watch than the situation itself, as the Kuwait-based worker found. He is in touch with his family almost every day, by phone and video call. During the conflict, they grew very worried after watching the news."They often told me that I should return to India as soon as possible and questioned why I needed to continue staying in Kuwait when the situation was uncertain," he said.He said he understood their concern but could not act on it. "I explained that leaving a job suddenly was not a practical option, especially during that difficult period when travelling was also very challenging," he said.Saad's family faces a similar tension. Calls are frequent, yet they cannot ease the distance. The family wants the couple home, but the fear of being unable to return keeps them from pressing the point.Behind these decisions lies a choice many Indian families in the Gulf know well. The man in Kuwait said his decision to stay or leave rests mainly on two things: the security situation and his professional responsibilities."If the situation becomes seriously unsafe, I would certainly consider returning to India," he said. "However, at present, things are gradually returning to normal, and I feel comfortable continuing my work here."The second factor is work at home. "Finding a job with a comparable salary and suitable working conditions in India is not easy. I have family responsibilities, so maintaining my employment and financial stability is very important," he said.For now, he intends to stay, and to visit his family when he can. "As long as the situation remains safe and stable, I would prefer to continue working in Kuwait. We also take our vacations from time to time and visit our families in India," he said.His reasoning reflects how many families weigh the risk. "Ultimately, our priority is safety, but we also have to think about our families, careers and financial responsibilities," he said.The latest suspension is due to run until November 30, but the pattern so far gives families little reason to plan around it. Air India's cancellation of Jeddah flights, which first ran until November 24, was extended to November 30 within days, and the other carriers have moved their dates in a similar way.For Saad's sister and her husband in Riyadh, and for thousands of others in the Gulf, the wait continues. A family emergency has been postponed, a festival has been missed, and a short flight home now means a long detour or no journey at all.Until the skies over the region settle, the suitcases stay packed.
Article Summary: Air India and Air India Express have extended the suspension of their flights to and from Jeddah until November 30. The other Indian carriers on the route have taken similar steps. For families on both sides of the route, the delay has meant missed visits, longer journeys and a constant worry.

Article Title: Florida man sentenced to 47 months in prison for using AI to clone streamer N3on’s voice and steal $260,000 in cryptocurrency from a meme coin project
Article Text:
Image: Left/David Sanchez/Port St. Lucie Department/Right/Streamer N3on @n3onsingh

AI voice cloning of N3on and fake accounts helped a Florida man steal $260,000 in cryptocurrency

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Mikyle "N3on" Rafiq (Image: @n3onsingh)

Who is streamer N3on, and why this is not his first brush with AI deepfakes and digital doubles

Florida man David Anthony Sanchez has been sentenced to 47 months in prison for using AI to clone the voice of streamer N3on and defraud a meme coin project of $260,000 in cryptocurrency . Sanchez, from Port St. Lucie and also known as “Dave the Jewler”, passed himself off as the popular online personality, persuading the project’s organisers that the streamer had agreed to back their plans. He pleaded guilty to two federal charges of money laundering and aggravated identity theft, and the court has also ordered him to pay restitution to the project’s victims on top of his prison term.According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida, court records show that Sanchez set up online accounts designed to look as though they belonged to N3on. He then used them to deal with the project’s organisers while playing two parts at once, the streamer himself and his representative.To make the story stick, he executed agreements in the streamer’s name and sent over a voice recording, generated with AI, that mimicked N3on to falsely confirm his involvement. Taken in, the victims transferred cryptocurrency to accounts Sanchez controlled. A substantial portion was later converted into US dollars through transactions designed to hide where the money came from and who owned it, and Sanchez spent it for his own benefit.The streamer at the centre of the case is Mikyle Rafiq, who goes by N3on online, Engadget reported. This wasn't his first encounter with a digital double. Citing Aftermath, the report said he once used a deepfake of himself to keep his Kick stream running around the clock.Acting US Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas used the sentencing to send a message. “Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm,” she said in the office’s statement. She added that Sanchez exploited AI to manipulate unsuspecting victims' trust, and that the sentence reflects a commitment to holding to account those who use emerging technologies to defraud others.US District Judge Melissa Damian imposed the term, which was announced on 24 November, following an investigation by the FBI’s Miami field office.
Article Summary: Florida man David Anthony Sanchez sentenced to 47 months in prison for using AI to clone the voice of streamer N3on and defraud a meme coin project of $260,000 in cryptocurrency. Sanchez, from Port St. Lucie, passed himself off as the popular online personality, persuading the project’s organisers that the streamer had agreed to back their plans.

Article Title: In 1969, a Missouri town buried a time capsule four feet underground; when it was opened 50 years later, floodwater had damaged most of its contents, but one mother’s letter to her daughters survived
Article Text:
AI Representation: In 1969, residents of Hannibal, Missouri, buried a time capsule during the city's 150th anniversary celebrations. Image credits: Chatgpt

Water damaged much of the collection

A letter to two sisters survived

Central Park historic district. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Hannibal prepared another capsule for 2069

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In 1969, residents of Hannibal, Missouri, buried a time capsule during the city's 150th anniversary celebrations. It contained photographs, letters and objects representing everyday life at the time. According to Hannibal Parks and Recreation, the capsule was placed four feet underground in Central Park. Fifty years later, staff opened it as part of Hannibal's bicentennial celebrations. They realised that there was water damage to many things inside, but there was one family letter that remained in perfect condition. This discovery provided a personal link to the history of the town and enabled two sisters the opportunity to read a message written by their parents many years ago.Hannibal Parks and Recreation Department staff opened the underground vault holding the time capsule on May 1, 2019, according to the department's own news release. They discovered about 40 plastic bags in the vault. The bags were mostly wet, while some bags had a lot of water in them. According to KHMO radio, staff pumped out about two feet of water from the vault prior to recovering items.Efforts were made to retrieve the items and dry them. Some were identified, but many others could not be. The water had impacted the pictures, letters and other materials. According to Hannibal Parks and Recreation, items reported at the time as going into the 1969 capsule included the dress worn by Hannibal's sesquicentennial baby, sesquicentennial editions of the Hannibal Courier-Post and the Quincy Herald-Whig and tapes of radio broadcasts from KHMO and KGRC. Several letters, photographs, souvenirs and other materials were in the collection, which was related to life in Hannibal in its sesquicentennial year.One of the recovered items was a letter written to Marilyn and Patricia Jurgens. The letter, dated July 6, 1969, came from their parents, who signed it "Daddy and Mama," the Hannibal Courier-Post reported. In addition to the letter, there were some photographs of the two girls. While Marilyn was a senior in high school, Patricia was in eighth grade when the letter was written. The letter stayed in the time capsule for 50 years until it was found by staff.Hannibal Parks and Recreation described how the letter appeared. In particular, the organisation noted that it was the only one in good condition among all the letters that used to be there. Some of them were still readable, but most were damaged. This provided the sisters with a chance to read the words of their parents after half a century, while the other items represented the history of the city. It recorded a private moment from 1969.The damage did not end the town's time capsule tradition. For its bicentennial celebrations in 2019, the city prepared a new capsule containing materials for future generations. People were invited to bring pictures, letters, yearbooks, club memorabilia and other materials that would show the life of Hannibal in 2019.Children even wrote letters to the people who will be living in Hannibal in 2069. The new capsule was sealed at a ceremony in Central Park on October 26, 2019. It is scheduled to stay unopened until 2069. The press release about the new time capsule, issued by the Hannibal Parks and Recreation Department, contained information and an invitation to residents. Water destroyed many of its components, but dozens of objects were rescued and identified. One thing, however, the Jurgens family letter, managed to convey the message of two parents to their daughters and link the event of 1969 with its discoverers in 2019.
Article Summary: In 1969, residents of Hannibal, Missouri, buried a time capsule during the city's 150th anniversary celebrations. It contained photographs, letters and objects representing everyday life at the time. Fifty years later, staff opened it as part of Hannibal's bicentennial celebrations. They realised that there was water damage to many things inside, but there was one family letter that remained in perfect condition. This provided two sisters the opportunity to read a message written by their parents many years ago.

Article Title: In 1964, Oklahoma City endured 1,253 sonic booms in six months; seven years later, Congress ended funding for the U.S. supersonic transport program amid cost, technical and environmental concerns
Article Text:
AI Representation: Oklahoma City became the centre of an unusual aviation experiment. Image credits: Chatgpt

Operation Bongo II brought repeated sonic booms over Oklahoma City

Sonic booms became a problem for commercial aviation

Skyline of Oklahoma City. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Congress ended the U.S. civilian SST program in 1971

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In 1964, Oklahoma City became the centre of an unusual aviation experiment. For six months, U.S. Air Force jets flew over the city at supersonic speeds, producing loud sonic booms to test whether people could tolerate the noise from future passenger aircraft. By the end of the experiment, 1,253 sonic booms had been generated over the area. The experiment, called Operation Bongo II, provided aviation experts with valuable information regarding the impact of sonic booms on houses and people living in them. At the same time, the experiment showed an increased level of public opposition to overland supersonic flights. Congress cut off funding for the American supersonic transport (SST) program in 1971.The Federal Aviation Agency (FAA) ran Operation Bongo II, which began on February 3, 1964. Oklahoma City was chosen because the region had been depending economically on the FAA's aeronautical facility and the Tinker Air Force Base. Scientists aimed to study the impact of the sonic booms on structures and also on how people could develop a tolerance to the sound.The aircraft and personnel for this study were provided by the U.S. Air Force. Aircraft such as the F-101, F-104, F-106 and B-58 flew over the city at supersonic speeds. The flights occurred up to eight times a day, seven days a week, for 26 weeks.This stage ended on July 31, while the observation stage followed for 13 weeks. A federal sonic boom research summary archived by the Defense Technical Information Center says nine control houses were part of the program, spread across different parts of the city. Two of those houses carried heavy instrumentation to track how the structures responded and two more homes outside the boom area were used to compare against natural wear. Other sensors recorded pressure changes and sonic waves. Residents reported sleep and conversation disruptions. Some also experienced cracked plaster and glass.Others associated the booms with the troubles of farm animals. From the survey results, it became evident that there was split public opinion regarding the issue. Around 73% of respondents claimed they could tolerate the booms in terms of their quality and intensity. However, 27% of the respondents claimed that they could not. Around 40% of the respondents claimed that the booms had caused some structural damage. But no significant structural damage was found in the FAA's instrumented control houses.The experiment was part of a wider attempt to design a commercial plane that would be able to travel faster than sound. The U.S. aimed to design a supersonic passenger jet that would be competitive with planes under development in Britain, France and the Soviet Union. The U.S. plane was meant to carry about 300 passengers at more than twice the speed of sound, according to the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum's archive on the program. The development of such an aircraft posed significant technical and economic difficulties. Technical problems included aerodynamics at high speeds, engine efficiency, fuel usage and heat generation by supersonic flight. The noise level posed additional problems.The supersonic jet produced shock waves reaching the ground as a sonic boom and their repeated occurrence would affect people's comfort and could cause damage to buildings. The Oklahoma City trial and earlier tests in St. Louis added to public and political opposition. NASA's history of sonic boom research explains that public pressure became a major challenge for the American SST effort. The paper traces how NASA's work moved from early boom measurement flights to a shaped sonic boom demonstrator, a modified F-5E built to test whether altering an aircraft's shape could reduce the pressure signature heard on the ground. It notes that the demonstrator was flown repeatedly over the Mojave Desert and the program helped establish the shape-focused design approach now central to quiet supersonic flight.The American supersonic transport effort received considerable criticism due to its high cost, delayed production and technical problems. Furthermore, environmental impacts and public acceptance of the sonic boom were concerns that reduced the credibility of the program. Congress cut funding for the U.S. civil SST project in 1971 and Boeing's historical archive lists March 24 as the date the project was cancelled.This move meant the proposed American passenger plane never got built. The termination of the program did not signify the end of supersonic flights in the country, since military jets were still capable of flying faster than the speed of sound.The cancellation of the American civil SST project did not signify the end of civilian supersonic flights anywhere around the world. Meanwhile, Britain and France pressed ahead with the Concorde, which entered commercial service in 1976. Operation Bongo II alone could not have brought the American SST program to its demise. Nevertheless, the results of the operation and the public response demonstrated how challenging it was to operate supersonic planes over populated areas.
Article Summary: Operation Bongo II brought repeated sonic booms over Oklahoma City. For six months, U.S. Air Force jets flew over the city at supersonic speeds. It was part of a wider attempt to design a commercial plane that would be able to travel faster than sound. By the end of the experiment, 1,253 booms had been generated over the area.

Article Title: In 1975, an Ohio couple collected 1,400 cans for a homemade solar furnace; sunlight warmed their home into the 70s, with oil heat used after the sun went down

Why homes were turning to the sun

Sunshine by day, oil after dark

Sunlight warmed an Ohio home into the 70s Fahrenheit in 1975, with oil heat used after dark (representative image). Image Credits: ChatGPT

What

NASA

engineers found about solar heating

Why one success story has limits
