What the story still teaches

In 1975, an Ohio couple gathered 1,400 cans to build a homemade solar furnace. According to a 1977 issue of The Worldwide News, sunlight warmed their home into the 70s Fahrenheit, or about 21 degrees to 26 degrees Celsius. Oil heat was used only after sunset. It might sound like some quirky experiment, but it reflects a time when ordinary households were looking for ways to keep their homes warm without relying on oil alone.The mid-1970s saw some tense years for energy markets. Yale University's Energy History website explained how the oil prices of 1973 and 1974 led to the price of gasoline and crude oil quadrupling. This was a source of concern for the future of energy in the nation. Solar power was seen as one of the more promising solutions for the future since it could be produced and used at the scale of a single home. In this context, the couple’s decision to collect cans to harness solar energy was part of a wider search for new answers.The most interesting part of the couple's story was how practical it was. The sun warmed the house into the 70s, and oil heat was used only after the sun had gone down.The oil system was not completely abandoned; it was a reserve for when there was no sun. This kind of mix makes sense, as the sun can't heat a home in the dark. The homemade furnace didn’t have to do all the work alone. It could take over the daytime work while oil covered the rest.Home solar heating was also receiving attention from experts. A technical memorandum from NASA's Langley Research Center outlined a low-cost solar heating system designed to supplement a homeowner's existing warm-air heating system. Tests of a demonstration system indicated that a homeowner could save about 40% of the heating costs if they had a 1,500-square-foot home with insulation to the 1974 FHA minimum standards. The figure applies to NASA's design and not to the furnace owned by the Ohio couple. The memorandum also added that homeowners couldn’t just choose a solar heating system from stock at a local heating contractor. This gap may help explain why some households tried to build their own systems.An important note of caution came from Yale’s Energy History website. Despite the high hopes, it observed solar energy in the 1970s had critical limitations. Many solar technologies were still highly experimental, small in scale, and unconventional in design, so the Ohio couple's result was a hopeful example, not a guarantee. Sunlight, house size, and insulation all play a role in how well a heating system performs.So results from one home cannot be assumed for another.Today, energy bills and climate worries are familiar topics for many young adults. So this story, more than 50 years later, still feels relevant. The couple saw an opportunity, gathered materials, and tried to find a practical solution. They also used oil heat after sunset instead of relying on the sun alone. The story shows how major changes in home heating can often begin with small experiments using something as simple as a can.
Article Summary: In 1975, an Ohio couple gathered 1,400 cans to build a homemade solar furnace. The sun warmed the house into the 70s, and oil heat was used only after the sun had gone down. The story shows how major changes in home heating can often begin with small experiments using something as simple as a can.

Article Title: In 1961, a California father buried a letter beneath the playhouse he built for his daughter; 58 years later, it surfaced decades after his death, and the girl he wrote to was now a grandmother
Article Text:
A representative scene of a backyard playhouse being taken down, with an old time capsule uncovered in the soil. Image Credits: ChatGPT

The playhouse that kept a secret

A representative image of a woman holding a decades-old handwritten letter, with a playhouse softly visible behind her. Image Credits: ChatGPT

The family that kept the capsule

A visit in late 2024

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Passing the memories on

A letter can sit in the dark for decades and still reach the right person. In 1961, a father in Northridge, California, wrote a letter to his daughter and buried it in the family backyard. ABC7 Los Angeles reported it was dated 26 November 1961 and marked the completion of a playhouse built by her father and grandfather. It remained hidden for 58 years until the playhouse was pulled down in 2019. By then, the girl it was written for had grown up, lost her father long ago, and become a grandmother herself.The girl in this story is Jacqueline Louise Bennett, who now goes by Lyn Campbell. She was an only child of her parents and lived in the Northridge house for 27 years. Her father and grandfather built the playhouse, and her father had buried the letter without telling anyone. She lost him when she was eight, and all her memories of him were connected to that house. She said it felt like he was still around her, and she described herself as a “daddy's girl. ” Even after she moved away, she came back from time to time to visit her old home and old school.The next chapter that began in 2019 was another family's. Grace Medrano and her husband were working on updating their backyard, and the work included tearing down the playhouse. Their contractor then found the time capsule. Medrano didn't toss it away. She thought it must have meant something to somebody and saved it as a small piece of the house's history. After the couple began their own family, she wanted to show it to her daughter as she grew older and tell her that the home once belonged to another little girl. Campbell later said the family didn't know her and had no reason to think that anyone connected with the house would ever turn up. The capsule stayed with the Medranos from 2019 until her visit, a gap of roughly five years.Campbell's visit came later in 2024. She got in touch with the current homeowners, and it was during that conversation that she learned about the capsule. She called the moment very emotional and wondered how Medrano was able to keep it.From her point of view, the family could have easily thrown it out. She also pointed out that the discovery was only made possible because the playhouse was torn down. If the playhouse had still been standing, no one would have known the letter was even there. ABC7 described the story as a feel-good holiday tale, more than 60 years in the making, and the capsule as a precious gift.For Campbell, the gift wasn't just for her. She showed the capsule to her son and grandson and said she was going to pass it on to them. She hoped that they would carry on her memories of the people and places that mattered most. This detail shapes the narrative. In 1961, a father hid a note for his only child. In 2019, a stranger saved it. Now a grandmother plans to pass it on to her family. In the end, a note buried in 1961 took more than 60 years to reach the little girl it was meant for.
Article Summary: In 1961, a father in Northridge, California, wrote a letter to his daughter and buried it in the family backyard. It remained hidden for 58 years until the playhouse was pulled down in 2019. By then, the girl it was written for had grown up, lost her father long ago, and become a grandmother herself.

Article Title: Around 60 Maryland landowners approach US Supreme Court to challenge a proposed 67-mile power line project; residents argue that a private energy company cannot enter their properties for surveys
Article Text:
Maryland landowners want US Supreme Court to intervene in MPRP dispute. Image Credit: FOX 45 News(Baltimore)

Maryland landowners challenged the 67-mile power line project

How the legal dispute reached the Supreme Court

US Supreme Court. Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons

The project raised concerns about data centre expansion

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Survey access has already affected landowners

Around 60 Maryland landowners have approached the US Supreme Court in an effort to stop a private energy company from entering their properties to conduct surveys for a proposed 67-mile electricity transmission line. The petition challenges lower court decisions that allowed PSEG Renewable Transmission to access private land before its authority to do so was established. The dispute centres on property rights, the use of eminent domain and whether a company can obtain court-ordered access while its proposed infrastructure project is still awaiting state approval.The dispute involves the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project (MPRP), a proposed transmission line that would pass through rural parts of Baltimore, Carroll and Frederick counties. The project is being developed by PSEG Renewable Transmission, a New Jersey-based energy company.According to Maryland Matters, 60 landowners filed a petition with the US Supreme Court on November 4, challenging decisions that allowed PSEG surveyors to enter their properties for field studies. The landowners are represented without charge by the Pacific Legal Foundation.The residents argue that PSEG should not be permitted to enter privately owned land until it has secured the necessary approval from Maryland regulators and established that it has the legal authority to exercise eminent domain.Eminent domain is the power that allows government authorities, and certain legally authorised entities, to acquire or access private property for public projects under specific conditions. The landowners' objection is that PSEG has been allowed to exercise powers associated with this authority without first demonstrating that it qualifies.The disagreement has been developing for several years, with resistance from property owners along the proposed transmission line route.In April 2025, PSEG filed a lawsuit against more than 100 landowners who had refused to allow survey teams onto their properties. The company maintained that Maryland law permitted entities with eminent domain authority to enter private land to collect information needed for proposed infrastructure projects.In June 2025, US District Court Judge Adam Abelson granted PSEG a preliminary injunction, allowing its surveyors to enter the disputed properties despite opposition from residents. A preliminary injunction is a temporary court order that permits or prevents certain actions while a legal dispute is being considered.The landowners subsequently challenged the decision, but the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit upheld the injunction in August 2026. As reported by FOX45 News, the appeals court decided that PSEG likely possessed the necessary eminent domain authority to conduct surveys before receiving its final state approval.The court's reasoning was linked to Maryland's regulatory process, which requires field studies and other technical information before the Public Service Commission can decide whether to approve the project.The landowners now want the Supreme Court to examine whether that reasoning allowed a private company to exercise disputed property access rights prematurely.Beyond the immediate disagreement over access to private land, the transmission line has become part of a wider debate about the growing demand for electricity from data centres in the region.The Washington Times, in its November 8 report, connected the landowners' Supreme Court challenge to concerns about the expansion of data centres in the metropolitan area. Residents argue that the proposed transmission infrastructure will help supply electricity to an increasing number of these facilities, which require substantial amounts of power to operate.The need for additional electricity has also been highlighted by regional grid operator PJM Interconnection. According to Maryland Matters, PJM considers the MPRP necessary to prevent problems with the region's electricity infrastructure, including potential blackouts. This comes as electricity demand from data centres continues to rise while some existing power plants are being retired.According to Maryland Matters, PSEG's fieldwork has included boundary surveys, assessments of forests and wetlands, habitat studies and acoustic surveys to identify bats. The company reported in September 2026 that only 9 archaeological surveys remained on properties involved in the original lawsuit.FOX45 News also reported that the dispute extended beyond permission to conduct surveys. PSEG sought additional restrictions preventing landowners from hunting on their properties during notified surveying periods.In one example detailed in the court petition, survey notices covered the period from September 29 to October 31, 2025, even though a land agent reportedly indicated that the actual survey work would require only one day. A federal judge granted restrictions requiring property owners to obtain written agreement from PSEG before hunting during those periods.According to FOX45 News, the Supreme Court has not yet agreed to hear the case. Meanwhile, the Maryland Piedmont Reliability Project(MPRP) remains under the state's regulatory review process.
Article Summary: Maryland landowners challenged the 67-mile power line project. The petition challenges lower court decisions that allowed PSEG Renewable Transmission to access private land. The dispute centres on property rights, the use of eminent domain and whether a company can obtain court-ordered access while its proposed infrastructure project is still awaiting state approval.

Article Title: In the 1860s, Bartholdi imagined a torch-bearing woman at the Suez Canal; the project stalled, but the concept helped inspire America’s Statue of Liberty
Article Text:
Before Lady Liberty, there was a lighthouse lady for Suez. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

A young sculptor who loved big things

The lighthouse that never rose

Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi, the French sculptor behind the Statue of Liberty, who first proposed a torch-bearing woman for the Suez Canal. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons

A new chance in a new country

How much of Egypt is in Lady Liberty?

A strong link, not a copy

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Most people know the Statue of Liberty from postcards, films, and holiday snaps. Few people know that her story may have begun in Egypt long before New York. Anthropologist Rebecca M. Joseph looked into the monument's early history in a National Park Service report . She found that the design almost certainly grew from an earlier idea. That idea was of a huge torch-bearing woman, which sculptor Auguste Bartholdi imagined as a lighthouse for Egypt’s Suez Canal in the 1860s.Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi was born in 1834 in Colmar, France. At the age of 20, he completed his first commission, which was a large bronze statue of a general. He also went to Egypt with a group of French cultural ambassadors. Their job was to photograph some ancient works. According to the National Park Service biography of Bartholdi , they found ruined cities in the desert, but the colossal statues were still standing there. This was what inspired the young artist. Joseph's report also recorded that he drew Egyptian women in 1856, and those sketches would matter later.By the late 1860s, the French were building the Suez Canal under the oversight and funding of Egypt's ruler, Khedive Isma’il Pasha. Bartholdi had a meeting with him. He had brought a small figure of a giant lighthouse. It showed an Egyptian peasant woman, or fellah, carrying a torch high to guide ships.Bartholdi called it ‘Egypt (or Progress) Carrying the Light to Asia.’ The khedive turned the design down, and the project stalled. The lighthouse was never built, but the idea did not die there.The next opportunity came to Bartholdi through Édouard de Laboulaye, a scholar and an abolitionist. Laboulaye suggested the idea of a gift of friendship from France to America. But then war got in the way. During the Franco-Prussian War, Bartholdi led a local regiment to defend his hometown. France lost, and Germany occupied Colmar. He then sailed to America. Soon after arriving in New York Harbour in June 1871, Bartholdi settled on his preferred spot on Bedloe’s Island in New York Harbour. Joseph's report suggested that the statue idea went back to 1870 or 1871. It called the 1865 dinner party story a legend.The statue's design, Joseph noted, almost certainly came from Bartholdi’s Egyptian idea. From that earlier plan, he had used his drawings of Egyptian women as models. A note from the park service added that scholars had named the same link. These are both tall women holding a torch high, and both were meant for busy waterways. Certain details did change. The report says Bartholdi replaced a broken shackle and chain in the statue's left hand with tablets marked 4 July 1776. This was what Laboulaye had asked for. The change signalled a message of liberty for all people.The report used careful words like “almost certainly.” The park service also states that the document’s release didn't mean it endorsed every conclusion in it. The report also tested a popular rumour that Liberty was supposed to be a black woman. However, no evidence was found that Laboulaye or Bartholdi meant that. So the Egyptian connection is a strong one, but it is a connection of designs.It doesn't mean that the statue was copied. The Suez plan may have been a dry run for Bartholdi to imagine a giant woman holding a torch, even though nobody paid for it. The completed statue was assembled in Paris, then disassembled and shipped to America. It was dedicated in 1886 in New York. Today, the Suez design is seen as part of how the Statue of Liberty took shape.
Article Summary: Anthropologist Rebecca M. Joseph looked into the monument's early history in a National Park Service report. She found that the design almost certainly grew from an earlier idea. That idea was of a torch-bearing woman, which sculptor Auguste Bartholdi imagined as a lighthouse for Egypt’s Suez Canal in the 1860s.

Article Title: Florida woman sends $1.8 million of elderly mother's money to man posing as French billionaire; court orders her to pay $5.5 million in brother's lawsuit
Article Text:
Representative image

Florida woman loses her mother's $1.8 million

What did the online man claim about the $420,000 payment?

Why did her brother take her to court?

What did the appeals court say about the mother's condition?

Why did the court uphold the $5.5 million judgment?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A Florida woman who transferred nearly $1.85 million belonging to her elderly mother to unknown recipients at the direction of a man posing as a French billionaire has lost an appeal against a $5.5 million judgment in a lawsuit brought by her brother. Kimberly S. Langston had been acting under a power of attorney when she moved the money from her mother's bank account into her own account before sending it elsewhere. She later told her brother, Michael R. Burrows, that she had been defrauded by the man she met online and had become romantically involved with. On November 25, 2026, Florida's Third District Court of Appeal upheld the trial court's judgment of $5,537,250 against her, finding that the undisputed evidence established exploitation of an elderly person.According to the appellate court's November 25 opinion, Langston and Burrows are siblings, and their dispute concerned the handling of their mother Sherry L. Burrows' finances.In June 2013, their mother signed a durable power of attorney naming her husband as her agent and Langston as his successor. At some point, Langston became her mother's agent under the arrangement.In March 2020, Langston emailed her brother informing him that she had been defrauded by a man she met on the internet who claimed to be French billionaire François-Henri Pinault.The court recorded that $1,845,740 belonging to their mother had disappeared. Langston had first transferred the money into her own personal bank account before sending it to unknown individuals at the direction of the online contact.During her deposition, she testified that she had become romantically involved with the man after meeting him online. She acknowledged that she had never met him in person or otherwise verified his identity while transferring her mother's money.The court's opinion also highlighted a particularly unusual transaction involving a purported agent of the man claiming to be Pinault.According to the trial court's findings, Langston used her mother's money to arrange a purported $420,000 payment for the release of the man's agent, who was allegedly stopped by US Customs. She was told that the money would be used to secure the agent's release.However, the payment was directed to an unknown person who supposedly would pay the amount to US Customs. The appellate court noted that there was no evidence establishing that the transaction was genuine.Langston also failed to carry out due diligence on the purported investments, obtain receipts or other proof of where the money was going, or verify the identity of the person she was communicating with.The court further noted that she continued transferring money despite receiving no returns from earlier purported investments.Michael Burrows filed a lawsuit against his sister over the handling of their mother's money. His claims included exploitation of an elderly person, civil theft, breach of a promissory note and unjust enrichment.He argued that Langston had misused the authority granted to her under the power of attorney by transferring their mother's money into her personal account and subsequently sending it to unknown recipients.The trial court granted Burrows' motion for summary judgment on the claims of elder exploitation and civil theft, awarding him $5,537,250.Langston challenged the decision, arguing that her brother had not provided sufficient admissible evidence to establish that their mother qualified as an elderly person under Florida law. She also disputed whether the evidence established the required intent to prove exploitation.In its November 25 ruling, the Third District Court of Appeal examined whether Sherry Burrows qualified as an elderly person under Florida's elder-exploitation law.Under the state's legislation, the definition includes a person aged 60 or older whose physical, mental or emotional condition impairs their ability to adequately provide for their own care or protection.The court found that the undisputed evidence established that Sherry was over 60 and had been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. It also referred to testimony about her memory problems, including instances when she forgot to take her medication.The judges cited a July 2019 message Langston had sent to the online impersonator in which she mentioned her mother's Alzheimer's diagnosis and described her difficulties.The court also noted that Sherry had wanted to return to Colorado, where she had previously lived, but was unable to do so because of her illness. Based on the evidence, the appeals court concluded that her condition impaired her ability to adequately care for and protect herself.Langston argued that the evidence did not establish whether she had deliberately exploited her mother or had merely acted negligently.However, the appeals court rejected that argument, explaining that a breach of fiduciary duty under Florida's elder-exploitation law can arise from either negligent or intentional conduct.The judges also observed that an agent acting under a power of attorney cannot simply transfer the principal's property into their own account. By moving her mother's money into her personal account before sending it elsewhere, Langston had abused her authority and breached her fiduciary duties.The court identified several other failures, including her inability to verify the online contact's identity, the absence of due diligence on the purported investments and her continued transfers despite growing doubts about the man's identity.Langston had argued that she verified the man's identity through a video chat. However, the court cited a subsequent message in which she expressed doubts, saying she believed the video might have been a recording of the real François-Henri Pinault rather than a live conversation.The appeals court concluded that the undisputed evidence established multiple grounds for finding that Langston had exploited her mother. It therefore affirmed the trial court's $5,537,250 judgment in Burrows' favour.
Article Summary: Kimberly S. Langston transferred nearly $1.85 million belonging to her elderly mother to unknown recipients at the direction of a man posing as a French billionaire. She later told her brother, Michael R. Burrows, that she had been defrauded by the man she met online and had become romantically involved with. Michael Burrows filed a lawsuit against his sister over the handling of their mother's money. His claims included exploitation of an elderly person, civil theft, breach of a promissory note and unjust enrichment.

Article Title: Adopted son of former Kentucky governor seeks financial support in parents' divorce, alleges years of mistreatment; court rejects claim but orders nearly $66,000 in legal fees
Article Text:
Image: AP

Why did the former Kentucky governor's adopted son seek financial support?

What did the judge say about the mistreatment allegations?

Court rejected his financial support request

Why were Matt and Glenna ordered to pay nearly $66,000?

Can Jonah still seek his father's help with higher education?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The adopted son of former Kentucky governor Matt Bevin has lost his bid for financial support from his parents in their divorce proceedings, but a Kentucky judge has ordered both of them to pay nearly $66,000 towards his legal fees. Jonah Bevin, 20, had intervened in his parents' divorce case, alleging years of neglect and mistreatment, including being sent to residential facilities as a teenager. In an order issued on November 25, Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela J. Johnson rejected his request for retroactive and future child support, finding no legal authority under Kentucky law allowing an adult child to establish such a claim independently. However, the judge found that both parents had acted in bad faith during the proceedings and ordered them to contribute towards his lawyers' fees.Jonah is one of four children adopted by Matt and Glenna Bevin from Ethiopia. The couple also have five biological children. Glenna filed for divorce in May 2023, and their divorce was finalised in March 2025.Jonah intervened in the divorce proceedings in May 2025, seeking financial support from his parents.He alleged that they had abandoned him at the age of 17 at the Atlantis Leadership Academy, a residential facility in Jamaica, where he and other young people were subjected to abuse and neglect.After the facility was closed by child-welfare authorities, Jonah was placed in the custody of Jamaican child-welfare authorities. He alleged that his parents failed to help secure his return to the US and that outside advocates assisted him. However, the judge's order records that Matt Bevin eventually paid to have his son flown back to the US from Jamaica.Jonah's lawyers also questioned the validity of his high-school diploma, arguing that it had been issued by an online academy that was not accredited. The judge noted that little evidence had been presented about his diploma and educational qualifications.The case attracted wider attention amid the controversy surrounding the troubled-teen residential treatment industry. Celebrity Paris Hilton travelled to Jamaica to show support for young people removed from the Atlantis Leadership Academy.During a hearing in July 2026, the court heard testimony from Jonah, his mother Glenna and child-welfare advocate Donna J. Post about his upbringing and experiences at residential facilities.The judge considered accounts of alleged abuse and neglect alongside testimony about Jonah's behaviour during his childhood. These included competing accounts from Jonah and his mother about the family's circumstances and his experiences at residential institutions.Glenna testified that Jonah had been difficult to manage and had sometimes displayed threatening and aggressive behaviour. She also said that Matt had largely handled family finances and made most of the decisions concerning their son's placements at residential facilities.The judge questioned the selection and quality of those institutions, observing that, based on the testimony, none appeared to be evidence-based mental-health programmes and that they had been selected through word of mouth.The court also noted that Matt had claimed Jonah possessed a high-school diploma from an accredited programme but had not provided the promised documentation to establish this.Judge Angela J. Johnson ruled that Kentucky law did not provide legal authority for Jonah to independently establish a child-support claim against his parents.The judge found that the law did not allow an adult child to initiate proceedings to establish retroactive or future child support for himself. She also concluded that the evidence presented was insufficient to determine an appropriate amount of financial support, even if such a claim had been legally available.Consequently, Jonah's request for retroactive and future child support was denied.Despite rejecting the support claim, the judge found that both parents had acted in bad faith during the discovery process, particularly over the disclosure of their financial information.According to the order, the parents had delayed providing financial documents and other information required during the proceedings. The judge found that their conduct was intended to delay and frustrate the case.The court ordered Matt to pay $47,216 towards Jonah's legal fees, while Glenna was directed to contribute $18,477.50. The combined award amounts to $65,693.50, with both payments due within 30 days of the order.The judge also noted that Jonah's lawyers had billed $66,693.50 for their work between March 2025 and September 2026, with $1,000 already paid.The judge also considered Jonah's request to enforce a provision in his parents' marital settlement agreement requiring Matt to fund each child's post-secondary education or equivalent training for up to four years.The court recognised Jonah as a third-party beneficiary of that provision, meaning he could potentially enforce the educational funding commitment against his father.However, the judge denied his request at this stage because Jonah had not applied to a post-secondary programme, formally requested the money from his father or demonstrated that Matt had breached the agreement.The ruling therefore leaves open the possibility of further proceedings over educational funding if Jonah meets the relevant conditions in the future.The November 25 order is described as final and appealable. While his request for child support has been rejected, the ruling leaves the education-funding provision open to potential enforcement in a subsequent proceeding.
Article Summary: Jonah Bevin, 20, is one of four children adopted by Matt and Glenna Bevin from Ethiopia. He intervened in the divorce proceedings in May 2025, seeking financial support from his parents. He alleged that they had abandoned him at the age of 17 at the Atlantis Leadership Academy, a residential facility in Jamaica. Judge Angela J. Johnson rejected his request for retroactive and future child support, finding no legal authority under Kentucky law allowing an adult child to establish such a claim.

Article Title: Meet Pittsburgh's 'Green Bean Man': 76-year-old wakes up at 2:45 am every Thanksgiving to cook 675 pounds of green beans for people in need; has kept the tradition alive for 30 years, saying volunteer
Article Text:
Image: CBS

How Don Waite became Pittsburgh's 'Green Bean Man'

675 pounds of green beans prepared before sunrise

'I get more than I give': Why Waite keeps returning

Light of Life's 74-year Thanksgiving tradition

Rising demand adds urgency to the mission's work

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A 76-year-old volunteer in Pittsburgh has continued an unusual Thanksgiving tradition for nearly three decades, preparing hundreds of pounds of green beans for people in need. Known locally as the 'Green Bean Man', Don Waite began his Thanksgiving volunteering at Light of Life Rescue Mission in 1996. On November 26, 2026, he arrived at 2:45 am to prepare 675 pounds of green beans using 13 pounds of butter for the organisation's holiday meal programme. His annual kitchen shift has become a familiar part of the mission's Thanksgiving effort, which provides food to people experiencing homelessness and food insecurity. Despite the early starts and enormous quantities involved, Waite says volunteering has given him more than he feels he has given in return.Waite's association with the Thanksgiving kitchen began in 1996, when he started volunteering at Light of Life Rescue Mission. Another volunteer initially showed him how to prepare the green beans. When that person was unavailable for a later Christmas meal, Waite was asked to take over the task.He agreed, and what began as a request to help with one meal gradually became an annual commitment. Over the years, the quantity of green beans he prepared grew, and the nickname 'Green Bean Man' became associated with his work.Local reports have documented the tradition across several years. In 2016, WTAE reported that Waite had already spent 20 years preparing green beans for the mission. By 2023, he was reportedly handling around 600 pounds for Thanksgiving.For the 2026 Thanksgiving meal, Waite began work at 2:45 am on November 26. He prepared 675 pounds of green beans, using 13 pounds of butter, at the mission's Ridge Recovery Place on Pittsburgh's North Shore.The Pittsburgh Post-Gazette reported that Waite wore a denim button-down shirt embroidered with his nickname, which he had owned for 25 years. He also joked that he was the only person who enjoyed eating green beans at 4 am.The quantity was part of the mission's wider Thanksgiving food effort, which included hot meals and dinner boxes for people across the Pittsburgh area.For Waite, the annual kitchen shift is not something he considers a burden. Speaking to WPXI in November 2026, he reflected on his three decades of volunteering and said: "I've never, in 30 years, walked away from here going, 'What a burden.'"He added: "I get more than I give."His remarks capture the personal meaning he attaches to the tradition. While the work involves an early start and preparing food on a large scale, Waite has continued to return because of the satisfaction he finds in helping others.Light of Life Rescue Mission has been providing Thanksgiving meals since 1952. Its 2026 holiday programme marked 74 years of serving people in need.The organisation's 2026 Thanksgiving programme included more than 1,200 hot meals, with food served at its Voeghtly Street Shelter and delivered to residents of local high-rise buildings. Around 700 people were expected at the shelter. Separately, 150 volunteers packed 3,000 Thanksgiving meal boxes, each designed to feed a family of eight and collectively reach approximately 24,000 people. The mission expected its overall holiday outreach to provide food to more than 25,000 people during the week.The Pittsburgh-based nonprofit also provides food, shelter and support to people experiencing homelessness, poverty and addiction. Its food pantry distributes groceries, including fresh produce, dairy products, proteins and dry goods, to families facing food insecurity.The Thanksgiving effort comes as Light of Life has reported increased demand for food assistance. By October 2026, its pantry had distributed more than 44,000 additional pounds of food compared with the total amount distributed during all of 2025.The organisation's work also includes support for people rebuilding their lives after addiction and those experiencing homelessness. During the Thanksgiving period, volunteers helped prepare meals and distribute winter supplies, including coats and hygiene kits.For Waite, the annual green bean preparation is one contribution to that wider effort. His three-decade commitment has become a recognisable part of the mission's holiday work, helping ensure that people who might otherwise spend Thanksgiving without a meal have food to share.
Article Summary: Don Waite, 76, began volunteering at Light of Life Rescue Mission in 1996. On November 26, 2026, he arrived at 2:45 am to prepare 675 pounds of green beans. His annual kitchen shift has become a familiar part of the mission's Thanksgiving effort, which provides food to people in need.

Article Title: Farhat Jabeen challenges gender norms as Pakistan's first female jet ski instructor

Farhat Jabeen, a 35-year-old mother of four, is challenging gender barriers in Pakistan’s water sports sector as a jet ski instructor at Kallar Kahar Lake, offering women visitors an opportunity to ride with a female instructor in a sport traditionally dominated by men.Gripping the handlebars, Jabeen executes sharp turns across the lake, sending water spraying into the air. Her work has made jet ski rides more accessible to women who may be reluctant to ride with male instructors because of conservative social customs."A woman should be brave," Jabeen told news agency AFP on the shores of the lake, around 125 kilometres south of Islamabad.She has spent the past two years taking women on jet ski tours and riding alongside other instructors. However, she said entering a male-dominated workplace was initially difficult."It was very difficult when I first came here for this job. Many objections were raised about me," she told AFP."Some said 'You're a woman, how will you work among men?'" she added.With guidance from a senior instructor, Jabeen spent a month learning to operate the jet ski and follow safety procedures. She now works up to 11 hours a day, inspecting boat engines, cleaning equipment and repairing damaged life jackets before taking visitors on rides.Despite the demanding schedule, she said her family helped her overcome fatigue."When I go home and meet my children in the evening, when I see them, all my tiredness goes away," she said.Instructor Tariq Mahmood told AFP that Jabeen's appointment had made it easier to accommodate women visitors. Ever since she joined, "it has become completely easy for us to send women to ride" with her, he said.Muhammad Abbas Ashraf, manager of Kallar Kahar's Tourism Development Corporation, said women had faced difficulties accessing jet ski rides before her appointment."When we first introduced the jet skis, women who visited here faced difficulties, because we could not have them sit with us and ride," he told AFP.Qamar-un-Nisa, a 50-year-old school principal who rode with Jabeen, praised the appointment. "Appointing a female instructor is a very admirable step," she told AFP.Jabeen urged women to seek employment despite social resistance, "There is nothing to be afraid of," she said.

At least four were killed and 14 others sustained injuries after a six-storey under-construction building came crashing down in Karachi on Wednesday, with rescue operations continuing on Thursday to locate 17 people feared buried under the debris.The incident took place in the Baloch Colony area of the Pakistani port city. Police said rescue workers had so far pulled 14 injured people from the wreckage, according to the Associated Press.Government official Nasrullah Abbasi said families had informed authorities that 17 people were unaccounted for following the collapse. Sindh chief minister Murad Ali Shah had raised concerns about the construction on Wednesday and promised action over the matter.At a high-level meeting on Thursday, Shah ordered the removal of Waseem Shamshad from his positions as Sindh local government secretary and director general of the Sindh Building Control Authority (SBCA).He also directed that Shamshad's services be returned to the federal government, a statement from the chief minister's office said.Shah further called for a recommendation to the Centre seeking Shamshad's suspension and a formal inquiry into the matter.Karachi Mayor Murtaza Wahab said the immediate focus remained on rescuing people trapped beneath the rubble, but did not disclose the number of those missing.More than a dozen officials were also removed from their positions on Thursday over alleged negligence, according to a government statement.According to AP, such incidents are frequent in Pakistan, where building regulations are often inadequately enforced and construction firms are known to use inferior materials or flout safety norms to reduce costs. Article Title: Why thousands are protesting in Karachi against Asim Munir's proposal to divide Sindh

Sindhi nationalist groups rally in Karachi, opposing alleged plans to divide Sindh and accusing Asim Munir of undermining the province's unity (Image credit: Ayaz Latif Palijo's X)

Thousands of people, including political leaders and activists from various Sindhi nationalist organisations, rallied in Karachi on Monday to oppose alleged moves to divide Sindh into new administrative units.The demonstration, organised by the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, accused Pakistan's Army Chief Asim Munir and Punjab of attempting to weaken Sindh's territorial unity, while raising concerns over alleged economic exploitation and control of the province's resources.The rally brought together several nationalist groups from different parts of Sindh, with opposition to the proposed administrative changes emerging as the central theme of the demonstration.According to a press release issued by the organisers, the rally was led by prominent nationalist leaders, including Riaz Chandio, Dr Niaz Kalani, Aslam Khairpuri and Nawaz Khan Zaunr, along with other senior political figures, ANI reported.Organisations participating in the demonstration included Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Bashir Khan), Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Aresar), Jeay Sindh Qaumparast Party and Jeay Sindh Qaumi Mahaz (Niaz Kalani).Activists of Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz (JSMM), which is not formally part of the Jeay Sindh Rahbar Committee, also joined the rally.The organisers accused Punjab and Pakistan's army Chief Asim Munir of pursuing attempts to weaken Sindh's historical, territorial and national unity through the creation of new administrative units. They alleged that the proposed changes were a pretext to fragment the province.Participants declared that they would not accept any division of Sindh and insisted that its historical and geographical unity must be protected.The organisers described Pakistan as an artificial theocratic state and alleged that Sindh had faced political subordination and economic exploitation since its incorporation into the country. They asserted that the Sindhi nation had historically existed as an ancient and sovereign community.The rally also highlighted allegations of exploitation of Sindh's natural resources and agricultural land. According to the organisers, millions of acres of ancestral agricultural land, coastal islands and reserves of oil, natural gas and coal had been taken over by Punjab and the Pakistani state apparatus.The demonstration was organised to register opposition to what the groups described as internal colonial control of Sindh and to mobilise support against any proposed administrative division of the province.In a separate announcement, the central body of Jeay Sindh Muttahida Mahaz (JSMM) said it would intensify its political struggle by launching an economic blockade targeting Punjab.According to the press release, the decision was taken during a meeting of the organisation's central leadership a day before the Karachi rally. JSMM announced plans to enforce a shutdown of highways and transit routes to disrupt supply lines to Punjab.The organisation also said its movement, initially focused on defending Sindh's territorial integrity, would be expanded into a campaign demanding the complete national independence of Sindhudesh.The press release said JSMM planned to mobilise the Sindhi population, particularly young people, for sustained political mobilisation and resistance towards achieving independence from what it described as Punjabi colonial occupation.

Article Title: LeT, JeM proxies exposed, ISI eyes revival of 19 dormant terror outfits in Jammu and Kashmir
Article Text:
How ISI plans to rebuild terror networks in J&K

19 dormant terror outfits on ISI radar

Local recruitment, infiltration among key concerns

Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir , with plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny from the security agencies, news agency IANS reported.Pakistan's ugly motive is to create a network of revived terror outfits that can operate without any apparent links to established Pakistan-based organisations such as the Lashkar-e-Taiba ( LeT ) and Jaish-e-Mohammed ( JeM ), according to officials cited by IANS.The Hafiz Saeed-led LeT has been operating through The Resistance Front (TRF), while Masood Azhar's JeM has been linked to proxy outfits such as the People's Anti-Fascist Front (PAFF), Kashmir Tigers (KT) and Lashkar-e-Mustafa.However, investigations by agencies such as the Jammu and Kashmir Police and the National Investigation Agency (NIA) have increasingly exposed the links between these outfits and their parent organisations. The agencies have gathered evidence indicating that the different names are being used to mask the involvement of the LeT and JeM.An official told IANS that the ISI has now advised these groups to reconnect with former members of terror organisations that have been inactive in Jammu and Kashmir for years.Several of these outfits emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when militancy was at its peak in the Valley. However, as the ISI concentrated its operations around the LeT, JeM and Hizbul Mujahideen, many smaller groups gradually became inactive.Some ran out of funds, while others lost their operatives to security force operations, the official said.According to data cited by IANS, Jammu and Kashmir currently has 10 active terror groups, while 19 outfits remain inactive. Among the dormant organisations are the Kashmir Jehad Force (KJF) and Tehrik-e-Jihad (TeJ).An Intelligence Bureau official said the ISI is likely to focus on locating former members of these groups and encouraging them to rebuild their networks."These members would be told to look out for potential recruits and then revive these terror groups. There would be no direct link between these groups and the existing terror outfits. This helps the ISI in covering its tracks when an investigation into a terror attack is launched," the official said.A major consideration behind the proposed strategy is that several of these organisations are homegrown rather than Pakistan-based. Their revival could make it more difficult for investigators to establish direct links with established terror outfits operating from across the border, the report said.The ISI is also expected to draw on the experience of former members in areas such as recruitment and logistics. Although many of them are now older, officials believe their knowledge of local networks could prove useful in rebuilding the outfits.The agency is likely to focus on recruiting local youth, while Pakistan continues to explore ways to increase infiltration into Jammu and Kashmir through multiple routes, an official told IANS.Another official said the ISI is keen to restore militant activity in the Valley. However, the recent killing of Lashkar commander Lateef Bhat has dealt a setback to its plans and could delay efforts to revive terror networks for some time.The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns, officials said.This would require security agencies to tackle not only possible terror operations but also coordinated attempts to influence public opinion through propaganda, adding to the security challenges in Jammu and Kashmir, the report said.
Article Summary: Pakistan's Inter-Services Intelligence ( ISI ) is exploring a shift in its strategy in Jammu and Kashmir. It plans to bring back dormant terror outfits in the Valley as its existing proxy groups face increased scrutiny. The revived groups could be used for both ground operations and information warfare, including disinformation and propaganda campaigns.

Article Title: Pakistan petrol pumps threaten nationwide shutdown, give govt 15 days to meet demands
Article Text:
Pakistan's fuel crisis fears grow as petrol dealers threaten nationwide shutdown

Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism, giving authorities 15 days to address their demands, according to a report by Dawn.The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers and rapidly depleting their working capital. The association warned that continued uncertainty could force petrol pumps to suspend operations, potentially triggering a law and order situation.Addressing a presser at the Karachi Press Club, PPDA chairman Malik Khuda Bakhsh, along with other association representatives, demanded that dealers' profit margins be raised to 8 per cent of the retail price. They also alleged that refineries had cut petrol and diesel supplies, with one refinery reportedly halting diesel supplies altogether, Dawn reported.The dealers claimed that they collectively contribute PKR 5.74 billion to the national exchequer every day and urged the government to take their financial concerns into account before introducing further changes to petroleum-related policies.Khuda Bakhsh said previous strike threats had been withdrawn following government intervention, but several demands remained unresolved.He argued that changing market conditions following the US-Iran war made it necessary for the authorities to reconsider the existing pricing arrangement, according to Dawn.Pakistan introduced the daily fuel pricing mechanism in July, citing volatility in international oil markets. Under the system, the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) announces revised petroleum prices every day.The PPDA has repeatedly opposed the arrangement, demanding a return to monthly or fortnightly price revisions. Earlier, another petroleum dealers' association had also postponed its nationwide strike following assurances from the petroleum minister that the daily pricing system would initially operate on a trial basis.In August, the government approved a 15.5 per cent increase in dealers' margins on petrol and high-speed diesel. The move raised the margin by PKR 1.34 per litre to PKR 9.98, effective September 1. However, the dealers' demand for an 8 per cent margin remains unresolved.
Article Summary: Pakistan's petroleum dealers have threatened to shut down petrol pumps across the country if the government fails to introduce a monthly fuel pricing mechanism. The Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association said frequent revisions in petroleum prices were causing serious financial difficulties for fuel retailers. The association warned that continued uncertainty could force petrol pumps to suspend operations.

Article Title: SCO: Pakistan set to invite India for culture ministers' meeting
Article Text:
The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

After participating in the SCO inaugural civilisational dialogue in New Delhi, Pakistan is now all set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. It will be interesting to see how India responds as no Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack.Significantly, Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit - where India is usually represented by PM Narendra Modi -next year in late August, after initially considering having it on August 14 – Pakistan's Independence Day. An August 14 summit is unlikely to have seen participation by India at any level.The only significant visit to Pakistan from India after the April 2025 Pahalgam attack was by MEA additional secretary Alok Dimri for a meeting of the SCO national coordinators in September – shortly after Pakistan assumed presidency – to firm up the calendar of events under Islamabad's stewardship.After what is officially called Meeting of Ministers of Culture (SCO-MMC), Pakistan will also host more high-profile meetings of the SCO defence and foreign ministers in the run up to the Islamabad summit in August.The meeting for cultural cooperation among SCO member-states in Pakistan is a relatively low-stakes event for India that keeps political commitments minimal, unlike the foreign and defence high-level gatherings which might raise the political temperature at home.The last minister to visit Pakistan was S Jaishankar for a meeting of the SCO foreign ministers' meeting in October 2024, well before Pahalgam.Amid criticism by the Opposition for hosting Pakistan minister Musadik Malik for the Modi-proposed civilisational dialogue last week, India reiterated there was no dilution of its position on the Indus Waters Treaty that was "put in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack. India has stressed that SCO cooperation should not be mistaken for bilateral thaw.The visit by Malik passed off smoothly without any bilateral friction as he adhered to the protocol of addressing multilateral SCO themes, rather than raising sensitive bilateral issues.While the key question remains whether Modi will travel to Islamabad for the SCO summit, Indian officials say such a visit is highly improbable at this stage. Any bilateral thaw that might result in Modi's visit requires, as far as India is concerned, a fundamental shift in Pakistan's position on cross-border terrorism.India is seeking tangible progress on its security concerns and doesn't want to create any optics of normalisation when these concerns remain unaddressed.The possibility of a senior minister, most likely Jaishankar, representing India is not ruled out. It would allow India to sustain its active engagement with the SCO, while not being seen as softening its Pakistan policy. Officials point to the fact that there's already a precedent for that. In 2024, it was Jaishankar who attended the heads of summit in Kazakhstan, filling in for the PM.
Article Summary: Pakistan is set to deliver an invitation to India for a meeting of the culture ministers it will host under its presidency of the Eurasian bloc early next year. No Indian minister has visited Pakistan since the Pahalgam terrorist attack. Islamabad is also preparing to host the SCO heads of state council summit next year in late August.

Article Title: Lahore tops global pollution ranking again as AQI crosses 500, eight Pakistan cities among worst
Article Text:
Choking under state neglect: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lahore once again ranked as the world's most polluted major city on Sunday morning, with its Air Quality Index (AQI) reaching 538, placing it in the hazardous category, according to Pakistani daily Dawn. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres, as severe smog continued to affect the province.Data from Swiss air quality monitoring platform IQAir showed Lahore at the top of the global major city ranking with an AQI of 538 between 9 am and 10 am. The reading exposed residents to severe health risks associated with hazardous air pollution.Karachi was further down the global ranking with an AQI of 180, followed by Cairo at 162.The pollution crisis extended beyond Lahore, with Kahna Nau in Lahore district recording the worst air quality in Pakistan at an AQI of 606. It was followed by Lahore at 538, Bahawalpur at 536, Sargodha at 392 and Gujranwala at 347, Dawn reported.Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Skardu, Faisalabad and Peshawar completed the list of the country's 10 most polluted cities.Lahore has repeatedly featured at the top of global pollution rankings in recent weeks.It recorded an AQI of 266 on Saturday evening, while the city had logged an hourly reading of 465 between 7 am and 8 am on Friday, as heavy smog affected several parts of Punjab.The continuing pollution has raised questions over the effectiveness of the Punjab administration's anti-smog measures. Lahore Traffic Police, however, has claimed that enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.Chief Traffic Officer Syed Abdul Rahim Shirazi said on Saturday that traffic personnel had issued challan tickets to 14,653 vehicles emitting smoke. Action was also taken against 10,306 vehicles transporting sand, soil and other materials without tarpaulin covers. Police penalised 31,618 unfit and dilapidated vehicles and took action against 272,760 overloaded vehicles, he added.Separately, enforcement squads from the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between January 1 and November 18, Dawn reported earlier this week. During this period, authorities demolished 1,429 kilns, sealed 968 and registered 1,248 FIRs against violators.Between September 1 and November 18, which covers the peak smog period, the department carried out 29,999 inspections, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs. It also imposed fines worth PKR 101.45 million.The scale of Pakistan's air pollution is also reflected in long-term data. The 2025 World Air Quality Report put the country's average PM2.5 concentration at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation's annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, Dawn reported.The report also placed Pakistan among the world's most polluted countries, with an average AQI of 156.Globally, indoor and outdoor air pollution together account for an estimated 8.1 million deaths annually, making air pollution the second-leading risk factor for mortality worldwide. Outdoor particulate matter alone is responsible for an estimated 4.7 million deaths.
Article Summary: Lahore once again ranks world’s most polluted city as AQI breaches 500. Eight cities in Punjab also featured among Pakistan's 10 most polluted urban centres. Lahore Traffic Police claims enforcement against vehicles contributing to air pollution has been stepped up.

Article Title: 4.0-magnitude earthquake strikes Pakistan near Afghanistan border

A 4.0-magnitude earthquake struck Pakistan on Sunday morning, with tremors recorded in the region, according to the National Centre for Seismology (NCS).The earthquake occurred at 9.18am IST at a depth of 13km, with its epicentre at latitude 32.794°N and longitude 69.745°E. Seven people were killed in a clash between two tribes over the ownership of a forest in Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, news agency PTI reported, quoting police Saturday.The incident took place around 10pm local time on Thursday at Bilija forest in Battagram district, when armed members of the Gilal and Kaloch tribes confronted each other, leading to an exchange of gunfire.According to police, armed men from the Kaloch tribe took positions and opened fire, prompting retaliation from the Gilal side. Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash.The two tribes have been involved in a longstanding dispute over the ownership of Bilija forest, which has continued for several decades and claimed several lives in the past, police said.The Gilal tribe is associated with the Allai valley in Battagram district, while the Kaloch community belongs to neighbouring Kohistan district.Police said repeated efforts by the administrations of both districts to resolve the dispute and bring the communities together had failed to produce a permanent solution.The latest clash has once again raised concerns over the law and order situation in Imran Khan 's stronghold Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
Article Summary: Four members of the Gilal tribe and three from the Kaloch tribe were killed in the clash. One militant was killed in an exchange of fire after a police van came under attack in Lakki Marwat district of Pakistan's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Friday.The attack took place near Khan Khel village, within the jurisdiction of Bargi police station, when militants targeted a police mobile van, police said acording to news agency PTI.Four police personnel, including Station House Officer (SHO) Shakir Khan, were travelling in the vehicle when it came under attack.Police retaliated, triggering an exchange of gunfire in which one militant was killed. All four police personnel escaped unhurt.Earlier, Pakistan's Chief of Army Staff Asim Munir expressed the "unwavering resolve" of security forces to eliminate terrorism during a visit to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Last week, ISPR said four security personnel, including a major, were killed while 24 militants were eliminated in intelligence-based operations (IBOs) in Balochistan and North Waziristan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.In separate operations conducted last week, security forces also killed 74 militants across Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.
Article Summary: Four police personnel, including Station House Officer (SHO) Shakir Khan, were travelling in the vehicle when it came under attack. All four police personnel escaped unhurt. Article Title: 'I call for Imran Khan's release': UN rights chief flags ex-Pakistan PM's health, jail conditions
Article Text:
UN steps up pressure on Pakistan over Imran Khan's detention

Amnesty raises concerns over Khan's health

Family members' detention draws scrutiny
